Regarding Burdock. Chapter XXIII.
Burdock is an herb having broad and thick leaves near the ground, having at the tips of its stalks certain thorny and prickly heads, but curved, which are accustomed to adhere to the clothes of passersby. Whence Isidore says in book XVII: "Burdock is so named because it has a stalk arranged near the ground, and it is called <term>philatropos</term> <gloss>human-loving</gloss> by the Greeks, because it adheres to the clothes of men due to its roughness, and it grows near walls; and it is called <term>philatropos</term>, i.e., loving man, because with a certain affection it seems to adhere to the clothes of a man." There is a double species of burdock, acute and round, arranged in the likeness of a horse's foot, so that by many it is called <term>vngula caballina</term> <gloss>coltsfoot</gloss>, and the leaves of both are of a horrible odor and taste alike, as Dioscorides says. But Pliny says in book XXVI: "There are many species of burdock and all are medicinal. For they cure the stings of scorpions, nor do they strike a man if he has been anointed with its juice. A decoction of its root helps the teeth and also strengthens them if it is held warm in the mouth. Its seed taken internally cures ailments of the stomach; it is useful for those vomiting blood and it assists in cases of dysentery; for its root taken with wine stops the flow of the bowels. But when given alone, it helps those with stones <note>kidney stones</note>. The whole herb crushed with lard is good for swellings." The verdict of Pliny, according to Platearius: burdock or dock is a warm and dry herb having the power of dissolving, relaxing, opening, and attenuating, and therefore it is valid against scabies, itching, herpes, and impetigo, and it draws out humors from the skin. It dissolves the hardness and swelling of abscesses; it is effective against cold dropsy and obstruction of the spleen. Its juice, when mixed with rue, purges the brain and rheumatic flow if taken in small quantity.

# On Lettuce. Chapter XXII.

Lettuce, as Isidore says, is so named from the exuberance of its milky humor, or because it fills nursing women with milk. In men, it restrains the movement of Venus <note>sexual desire</note>. Its species is twofold: namely, domestic and wild, which we call <term>feralia</term> <gloss>wild/brutal</gloss>, because its back has hard prickles like iron, as Isidore says in book 17, in the last chapter. Regarding this, Pliny says in his *Dietary*: the wild lettuce is similar in form to the domestic, but it has longer, finer, rougher, and less green leaves on account of the scarcity of its moisture, and therefore it has much bitterness and astringency compared to the one that is domestic, because it is of greater heat and dryness. For this reason, many say that it provokes menstruation and expels raw humors, as Dioscorides says. 

Lettuce, for its part, is cold and moist in the second degree, and in neither quality does it exceed the measure, and therefore its use is of great medicine. It is subtle and moderate and, if it is fresh, it is quickly digested; it calms the burning and biting of the stomach and red bile, cools the ebullition of blood, and pacifies sleeplessness. It heals headache and choleric fumes, multiplies milk in women, and generates and increases semen in men. This occurs on account of the goodness of the blood that it generates in perfect quantity and at a perfect age. But when it becomes old and hard, its moisture diminishes and it turns bitter, and through its use, very bad blood is generated. The animal virtue <note>the capacity of the soul to govern the body through the senses</note> fails and is weakened; the cause of this is the mortification of the animal sense, because with its astringency, it suffocates the natural spirit. Therefore, such lettuce is most harmful to those wishing to generate, for it congeals the material and coagulates the seminal fluid, especially if its seed is consumed often in food or drink. This is the doctrine of Isaac in his *Dietary*. 

Pliny, however, in book 20, chapter 8, says about lettuce: there is a species of lettuce growing spontaneously which they call <term>caprina</term> <gloss>goats’ lettuce</gloss>, which, if thrown into the sea, kills fish that are nearby. With its stalk and obtuse leaves and crude salt, incised nerves are healed. Another species of lettuce grows in fields, whose leaves, crushed and applied with polenta, heal ulcers, and this the Greeks call <term>ysopon</term> <gloss>hyssop</gloss>. A third species grows in forests, which they call <term>steraton</term> <gloss>wild lettuce</gloss>, whose crushed leaves heal festering wounds; with the root and leaves, they mitigate holy fire <note>erysipelas</note>. There is also another species of this lettuce, round and short, which many call <term>beratia</term> <gloss>likely a variant of verrucaria/wart-wort</gloss>, whose juice hawks, by scratching the herb, extract and, by staining their eyes with it, dispel obscurity and cataracts when they grow old. The juice of this herb heals eye ailments, especially when mother's milk is mixed with it. It cures the bites of serpents and the stings of scorpions if its juice is drunk with wine and the crushed leaves are applied to the wound as a plaster. It also dispels and suppresses every swelling. The seed of lettuce, both wild and domestic, suppresses the imaginations of lust in sleep, and does not allow the body to be polluted if it is consumed frequently in food. Frequent and excessive use of it, however, causes obscurity in the eyes. Pliny attributes many other praises to it in the same chapter, but these shall suffice.

# On Burdock. Chapter XXIII.

Burdock is an herb having broad and thick leaves around the ground, having at the tops of its stalks certain thorny and prickly little heads, but recurved, which are accustomed to adhere to the garments of those passing by. Hence Isidore says in book 17: burdock is so called because it has stalks arranged toward the ground, and it is called <term>philatropos</term> <gloss>man-loving</gloss> by the Greeks, because it adheres to the clothes of men on account of its roughness. It grows near walls, and it is named <term>philatropos</term>, that is, loving man, because it seems to adhere to men's clothes with a certain affection. 

The species of burdock are twofold: sharp and round, arranged in the likeness of a horse's foot, wherefore by many it is called <term>vngula caballina</term> <gloss>horse-hoof</gloss>. The leaves of both are of a horrible odor and taste alike, as Dioscorides says. But Pliny, in book 26, says there are many species of burdock and all are medicinal. For they cure the stings of scorpions, and they do not strike a man if he has been anointed with its juice. The decoction of its root aids the teeth and also strengthens them if held warm in the mouth. Its seed consumed within cures stomach ailments, and to those vomiting blood, it is beneficial and aids in dysentery; for its root with wine stops the flow of the bowels, but taken alone, it helps those with stones. The whole herb crushed with lard is valuable for scrofula. Therefore, it is valuable against mange, itching, <term>ferpigine</term> <gloss>herpes/rash</gloss>, and impetigo. ### Chapter Eight: On the nature and admixture of gold.

**S**Objection must also be made against those who speak of the nature of gold, which alone, according to <term>Hermes</term>, is that in which no disease appears. For neither part of its material is infected or intemperate. Since, like all other things, it is composed of <term>sulfur</term> and <term>quicksilver</term> <gloss>mercury</gloss>, its sulfur is most lucid and pure, and through the strongest washings, it has been brought to a purity that possesses no combustible greasiness at all, nor any evaporable phlegmatic watery humidity. Perhaps in concave places, where the solid surface is often sublimated and digested by a temperate heat—a digestion that is called <term>pepansis</term> <gloss>ripening</gloss>—the earthy substance that is incorporated into the sulfur is clean and most subtle, vaporously suspended throughout the entire substance of the radical humidity of that sulfur. For this reason, it follows that the heat of that sulfur is constitutional, departing in no way from the temperament, and this is like the masculine virtue in the composition of gold. 

Similarly, its quicksilver has two substances purified to their extremes. For the third element, which is in the heat itself, is subtilized—not only materially divided, but vaporously—and is the most subtle earth, often sublimated in the cavities of the earth by the life-giving heat of the sun and the stars. Likewise, the watery element is also subtilized by the same method of repeated subtilization; and when glass is thus present, it subtilizes subtly. It is established that when these are mixed together by heat and the disposition of a place that produces and reflects the vapor upon itself, they are bound by the strongest bond of mixture. 

However, sulfur does not enter into the composition of gold merely by quality, but by substance; and since it is subtle, it will penetrate the substance everywhere through the quicksilver and, by coagulating, color it. And since both have been brought by sublimation to the form of the superior elements, which in the nature of transparency always reach a perpetual body, both will possess the fullness of purity. And when the many parts of the matter are thickened, they will exist together; for this is the property of a subtle substance, that which remains through coagulation will have many parts in a very small space. 

Therefore, the contracted transparency will create a citrine color, and the subtlety creates a great "leafing" <note>likely referring to the creation of gold leaf or the lamellar structure of precious metals</note>, and the constancy of many parts together in a small place and position creates weight, as is proven by those things which have been reasonably demonstrated regarding the heavens and the world. It remains, therefore, because of the "leafing" and the temperament together, that gold is little evaporable or not at all; for this reason, it is as if it has no odor. Although an odor is not essentially a smoky evaporation, a strong odor is nevertheless frequently found with a smoky evaporation, because of which it further follows that gold is more incorruptible than any metal and more able to withstand fire because of its most strong commixture in the mixture. For a smoky evaporation indicates a certain corruption of bodies, which is less in silver and more in copper. From these facts, one has the cause of why things like sulfur, arsenic, and certain others burn silver but do not burn gold. The cause of this—

<margin>Why gold is heavy.</margin>
<margin>Why gold does not burn.</margin>

<column-break/>

kind of thing is the mixture, in that all its earthly part is in the humidity, defending itself from burning, and all its humidity is in the earthly part, holding itself back so it does not fly away through evaporation. This connection is called <term>plō-fedus</term> <gloss>a "knot" or bond of elements</gloss> by <term>Plato</term>, and the "glue of the Germans" by <term>Empedocles</term>. 

From the temperance of gold, it is understood why it is hot and moist, conferring health against the trembling of the heart and melancholy, which makes one sad. And because of this, it confers benefits against those things that make a man talk to himself alone. It is beneficial against these passions whether the gold is rubbed upon the afflicted part or even taken and ground up. Because of its solidity, it is such that it does not soil the bodies it touches, except with difficulty, and for this reason, it is worn in rings and other ornaments. Silver, however, stains a little, and other metals stain much, which the gold does not do; this is because the greasy humor is separated in its entirety from them, to which the burnt earth is admixed in them, and this smears like the soot of a greasy body. 

However, the great purity of the matter causes it to be very rarely found admixed with other bodies, but always as if pure, which, when it cannot mix with others, cannot retain such purity, and for this reason, it degenerates into copper. Conversely, it is very rarely found unless incorporated into stones. And this, again, is why it is found as grains of sand frequently, because such purity must be scarce and raised from that matter and as if expelled, and therefore distinct; yet it is already found as a grain of <term>marchasita</term> <gloss>pyrite or mineral ore</gloss> together with it. From these facts, it is again clear why these two metals, namely gold and silver, were chosen for the material of coinage by the ancient wise men. They possess this special benefit for helping and comforting the human constitution, and they are more durable and noble than the rest. 

The things that purify gold are sharp and very dry, such as salts, and especially sea salts and the soot of greasy but dry bodies, and ground brick. When gold is to be purified, a clay vessel is made in the manner of a gourd or a bowl. Above that vessel, another similar to it is made, and it is glued at the place of the contacts with tenacious clay, which the alchemists call "the clay of the wise." In the upper part, there are many holes through which the vapor and smoke may exit, and afterwards, the gold is thinned into short and thin leaves and arranged in the vessel. This vessel, placed in the fire, does not diminish from the fire by sensible consumption. Nevertheless, in other ways, the clay of the wise is prepared in alchemy, but that which goldsmiths use suffices here. Thus, therefore, gold is purified, and nothing is burnt out in it except the ignoble substance, because of which <term>Hermes</term> elegantly says in his alchemical works: "Sulfur itself, by a certain subtle affinity of sulfur to which all metals are near, burns and incinerates all their bodies, but not gold; for its pores are tight and indissoluble." the single judgment of our CORNERUS regarding me shall protect me, just as the shield of Ajax easily protected Teucer, so that I might not be attacked, in my innocence, by the bites of envy or the barkings of slander from ill-natured men, of whom the earth and sea are full. Indeed, this shall gain me your goodwill, O AUDIENCE; this shall ensure your attention, so that you may receive with your customary kindness the reason for my appearance upon this stage, just as you receive it with your minds and ears. And so I plant my foot here, and I am content with this one thing: that if I say nothing more, you may know there are many other reasons favoring this act of mine. I shall consider the entire cause of my speech to be stated, and it shall be as if nothing had been said, should anyone anxiously, but in vain, search for another.

Nor shall I, in this philosophical assembly, prepare a long speech about PHILOSOPHY in general, which is truly a gift of GOD and the sweetest food for the soul. I have not resolved to speak specifically about its parts and supports, nor do I intend to pursue its utilities and praises; lest I be thought to repeat what has already been done, and to write an Iliad after Homer, the fountainhead of all talent.

I speak instead of ANTIPATHY, or the loathing, nausea, abstinence, and hatred of certain foods and drinks, and of the cause of this wondrous contradiction, so that I may not be entirely <term>ἀσύμβολος</term> <gloss>without contribution or empty-handed</gloss>.

For we see that not a few people sitting at the table with us abstain entirely from meat and fish. We see that they do not taste wine, beer, milk, or honey, and do not touch cheese, butter, or apples. And there are those who cannot digest strawberries, garlic, or eggs, nor can they endure the scent of a ROSE or an APPLE. We see these things, I say, O Audience, we see them all. But those who have explained the cause here—a cause, I say, that is adequate, necessary, and sufficient—are rare. And if I were to say there are almost none, I would certainly say nothing wrong, nor would I speak against the truth.

**notheia** <gloss>illegitimacy</gloss>. That which is given to illegitimate children from their paternal inheritance is called this; it was [limited] up to one thousand drachmas. **nomisma** <gloss>currency</gloss>, signifies two things: a legal custom, as *Aristophanes* in *Clouds* <gloss>249</gloss>: "We have no currency," and the stamping of minted copper. The Byzantines used thin currency.

**nomizomenōn** <gloss>of things managed lawfully</gloss>; "He cast in marked gold coins, and in some, tetradrachms of those conspicuously in circulation." And again, "Four thousand talents of the copper in circulation in Alexandria."

**nomographoi** <gloss>law-writers</gloss> <note>refers to the Roman Decemviri</note>. Among the Romans, in the three hundred and first year after the founding of the city, the office of the consuls having been dissolved, ten law-writers were entrusted with the protection of public affairs. They, for a certain time interpreting [laws] for the benefit and pleasure of the citizens, seemed moderate and most suitable of all to rule. For these men, having written the ten tablets in both the native and Greek laws, set them up on the so-called *kyrbeis* <gloss>pillars</gloss>. In the second year of their leadership, having incurred the accusation of tyrannical harshness, they were dissolved, as *Appius* in particular stirred the multitude to hatred against the decemvirate, he who plotted to ruin a virgin daughter of a certain man of no obscure military standing, having become gripped by a hot passion for the girl. The father killed her with his own hand, fearing the tyranny of *Appius*, for he was ripe to defile the girl by force. At this, the entire military was stirred and stripped the ten [men] of their power, and forced them to pay penalties for the injustices committed during their term of office.

**nomothesia** <gloss>legislation</gloss>, the setting of a law.

**nomothetai** <gloss>lawgivers</gloss>. Of old, *Moses*, but afterwards *Christ Jesus*.

The nature of some good thing from the outside. But not even these things [are enough], such as preparing against the enemy or being tripped up by others, the neighbors, or even by the neighbors' own agreements <note>original: "συνθηκῶν"</note>. Therefore, when it is reported that the enemies are preparing against us, it is necessary first to place oneself in safety, just as was said before, regarding the cities and the regions. Then, one must also aim for the desperate act, observing the strange things <note>original: "ἀλλαγαλίσα"</note> and the specific places through which they intend to pass, so that the agreements might be, for us, an ambush or an open war and profitable for us. But [regarding] what we might lose or eat, such as when we are campaigning with others and it is reported to us that the enemies are with us, it is profitable for us to be troubled by the fighting; likewise, if others are campaigning [among them], whether it is civil war or the neighbors are quiet, [one must] pacify that, for those who are fighting usually make peace for their own sake, observing the foreigners. But it is necessary to be neighbors, so that those who have descended for each of these might render the familiarity <note>original: "μυσάγωγία"</note> of their own knowledge. Both [must be] neighbors to each other, having acted safely as is necessary for all of them to plan, and if and in what manner, [in] the place inside [there is] only the marketplace, through which many of our own and the foreigners come up, looking toward the trade. For in this, they will be able to take the enemies more easily. Wherefore, as the day progresses, again they themselves [bring] the others, [and] the wars <note>original: "πολέμους"</note> exchanging and showing to us what—in my hymn—the enemies are called, and how those things of theirs are most hostile. It is necessary for all those who are commanding not to be of the same race as the opponents, nor to have suffered any great evil at our hands <margin>killing others</margin> [such as] if women or children or parents or brothers [were killed] by us there, for the longing for them would cause [the defector] in any place to wish to allow the enemies, and not otherwise plot against their own [people]. It is necessary for them to be prudent in nature, the ones who know how to fight in the places where they are said to be, having chosen this well <margin>fifth plate</margin>, prepared of them. Then [they must be] experienced in the places through which they will pass. It is necessary, too, that they be present...

For those under thirty years of age are stronger than the others. Taken up by stone mortars, they crush them with solid pestles until they produce the largest part, similar to vetch. **XL.** Virtue possesses the property of being of divine origin (1); for these three parts of it together constitute true virtue, and each one is always found joined with the other two. And indeed, in prudence there is also fortitude, in that the mind labors and exerts itself in searching for the truth, and does not rest until it finds it; there is also temperance, as it is a wise thing to be ignorant of certain things. In temperance, then, one finds prudence, which advises us not to neglect the things useful to life, so as not to suffer detriment; and for this reason, Medicine is of divine origin, because it is dictated by this eternal truth; there is also fortitude, so that one may know how to keep oneself far from pleasures. Indeed, in prudence, fortitude is present, so that it may labor in searching for the truth, and not rest unless it is explored; temperance is also present, by which it is wisdom to ignore certain things. In temperance, prudence is also present, so that one may not abstain from things useful to life even to one's own destruction: hence the origin of Medicine is divine; for it is dictated by this eternal truth: fortitude is also present, so that one may sustain temperance from pleasures. In fortitude, prudence is present, so that it may fight for the honest; temperance is also present, by which the victors do not wish to destroy those whom they can save, having been conquered.

<-*True virtue.*->

**XLI.** Therefore, no virtue is solitary, and where one is truly present, all others are present as companions: for it is barely the case that isolated virtues, to speak with the Divine Augustine <note>original: "(2)"</note>, deserve the name of virtues.

<-*Divine grace.*->

**XLII.** But that virtue, which is the one true one, and because it is true, excels all virtues, does not

<note>(1) Regarding which, Chap. III.</note>
<note>(2) Epistle CLXVII; otherwise XXIX, to Jerome, chap. 3, n. 11, and chap. 4, n. 14, Vol. II in the Paris Edition.</note>

<summary>The text defines virtue as having a divine origin and argues that prudence, fortitude, and temperance are inseparable components of true virtue. It asserts that isolated virtues are incomplete and concludes by introducing the concept of divine grace.</summary>

### CANTO XXI. OF THE SECOND CANTICA OF DANTE.

A noble subject, and nobly treated in this twenty-first canto. In it, the author sets forth how, as they continued their journey, they were rejoined by a soul, from whom they understood the reason for the shaking of the mountain and the singing of the souls. And finally, they recognized that this person had been a poet, and in supreme joy, Virgil recognized him.

<column-break/>

<note>A large historiated initial 'L' containing a scene with two figures in a landscape, representing the meeting of Dante and Virgil with the spirit of Statius. The initial is framed in a square border with decorative elements.</note>

The natural thirst that is never sated
except with the water, for which the young
Samaritan woman asked for the grace,
Was making me yearn, and the haste was spurring me
along the encumbered path behind my guide,
and I was grieving for the just retribution.
And behold, just as Luke describes for us
that Christ appeared to two who were on the way,
already out of the sepulchral tomb,
So an image appeared to us, and it was coming behind us,
looking down at the crowd that lies there,
nor did we notice it until it spoke first,
Saying, "My brothers, may God give you peace."
We turned suddenly, and Virgil
returned to him the sign that is fitting.

<column-break/>

THE NATURAL THIRST. He demonstrates that there is, as mentioned above, an innate thirst and desire in man for knowledge. And because the cognition of divine things is that through which we are blessed, and we cannot have this perfectly through our own industry, nor by a natural path, unless we are illuminated by the Holy Spirit—which Christ signified in the Gospel of Saint John, chapter 4, when, asking the Samaritan woman for a drink at the well of Jacob, and she denying it to him, alleging that the Jews do not associate with the Samaritans, he replied: "If you knew who it is that asks you for a drink, you would ask him, and he would give you a drink of the water of a spring that flows into eternal life." The young woman, therefore, after many words asked him, and Christ filled her with the Holy Spirit. For this reason, the poet very wisely demonstrates here that the natural thirst, that is, the natural desire to know and understand, is never sated except with the water; where the young Samaritan woman asked for the grace, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit. WAS MAKING ME YEARN. This is a metaphor derived from threshed grain, which is worked, that is, passed from sieve to sieve, so that it remains purged and clean; just so, our soul, wishing to find the truth, purges itself from time to time. AND THE HASTE WAS SPURRING ME demonstrates that at the same time, the soul was desirous of investigating the reason for the shaking of the mountain and the singing of the souls, and the body had to hasten in following its journey. But Statius, upon arriving, explains that which neither Dante, that is, the senses, nor Virgil, that is, the human intellect (even if illuminated by much doctrine), could understand by themselves. But Statius, who is accustomed to such things, explains them. And he posits Statius as the human intellect, which extends itself to understand that which cannot be understood by way of reason. And by comparison, he demonstrates according to what Luke writes in the twenty-third chapter.

<summary>This page marks the introduction of the poet Statius in Canto XXI, following an earthquake on the mountain. Landino interprets the "natural thirst" for knowledge through the biblical encounter between Christ and the Samaritan woman, framing human reason and divine grace as necessary components for understanding spiritual truths.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...as they appear near the sun.</meta>

If the sun has a yellow <term>zhi</term> <gloss>straight pillar</gloss>, the monarch is firmly established but the ministers will act independently. If a blue-red <term>zhi</term> <gloss>straight pillar</gloss> appears, the ministers will act independently and fail. If the appearance is yellow, white, and moist or glossy, success follows.

If blue and red vapors appear in a shape like two straight lines intersecting above, below, to the left, or to the right of the sun, this is called <term>jiaojiaoyin</term> <gloss>intersecting licentious vapors</gloss>. This vapor indicates licentious behavior. If there are intersecting red clouds beside the sun, there will be warfare beneath them.

If two vapors beside the sun intersect, pierce through one another, or face back-to-back, all these signify that great warfare will arise in the world, and there will also be internal rebellion and lack of harmony within the military. It is also said that if there are intersecting lines beside the sun, the side towards which the intersection strikes will be victorious.

If various vapors form a shape like the character for "mouth" <term>kou</term> <gloss>mouth</gloss> at the edge of the sun, this is called a **Sun Mouth**. One or two "mouths" indicate treacherous and harmful people. Three, four, or five "mouths" indicate that princes and nobles are plotting to seize the throne.

<summary>This passage details the interpretations of solar phenomena such as intersecting vapors and the appearance of "mouth" shapes, linking them to internal unrest, military conflict, and political conspiracies.</summary>
<keywords>solar divination, intersecting vapors, Sun Mouth, military conflict, internal rebellion, political conspiracy, portents</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...as they desire to declare themselves independent rulers. The following section describes specific atmospheric phenomena involving color and shape variations around the sun.</meta>

If the sun has a yellow straight pillar, the sovereign establishes his authority, and the ministers are loyal. If a blue-red pillar appears, a minister will declare independence.

If the straight pillar is red in the center and blue on the outside, a self-declared ruler will not succeed. If it is yellow-white, moist, and lustrous, the ruler will succeed.

When blue and red vapors appear in a shape like two straight lines intersecting above, below, or to the sides of the sun, this is called a **Cross-Intersection** <term>original: *Jiao* (交)</term>, which signifies licentiousness. This vapor signifies licentious conduct. If a cross-shaped red cloud appears beside the sun, there will be military conflict below it.

If two vapors appear on either side of the sun, intersecting, passing through each other, or facing away from each other, it signifies that a great military conflict will arise throughout the world. It also indicates internal turmoil and a lack of unity within the army. It is also said that if there is a cross-shaped vapor beside the sun, the side towards which the intersection points will be victorious.

If vapors arise in a shape like the character for "mouth" <term>original: *kou* (口)</term> at the edge of the sun, it is called a **Sun-Mouth** <term>original: *ri kou* (日口)</term>. If one or two "mouths" appear, it signifies treacherous and harmful people. If three, four, or five "mouths" appear, it indicates that feudal lords or princes are plotting to establish themselves as rulers.

<summary>This page details the divinatory interpretations of various solar atmospheric phenomena, including vertical pillars, intersecting vapors, and mouth-shaped formations, linking them to ministerial loyalty, internal rebellion, and political conspiracies.</summary>
<keywords>solar divination, straight pillar, cross-intersection, licentiousness, Sun-Mouth, rebellion, feudal lords, military conflict</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>

If a yellow straight pillar appears by the sun, the minister will rebel against the sovereign. If a blue and red straight pillar appears, the minister will declare independence.

If the straight pillar is red in the center and blue on the outside, the one who declares independence will not succeed. If it is yellow and white and appears moist and lustrous, the one who declares independence will succeed.

When the appearance of blue and red vapors resembles two straight lines crossing each other, whether above, below, to the left, or to the right of the sun, this is called a **Crossed Vapor** <term>original: *Jiao* (交)</term>, which signifies lewd conduct. If these vapors are accompanied by a lewd atmosphere, it indicates licentious behavior. If there is a crossed red cloud beside the sun, there will be military conflict below it.

If there are two vapors on either side of the sun that cross, penetrate, or face back-to-back, all these signify that great military conflict will arise under heaven. It also indicates internal rebellion and discord within the army. It is also said that if there is a cross beside the sun, the side that attacks from the direction of the cross will be victorious.

If various vapors appear in the shape of the character for "mouth" <term>original: *kou* (口)</term> at the edge of the sun, it is called a **Sun Mouth**. One or two "mouths" indicate treacherous and harmful people. Three, four, or five "mouths" indicate that princes and lords are plotting to establish their own rule.

<summary>This page continues the interpretation of solar atmospheric phenomena, specifically defining "Crossed Vapors" as omens of military instability and internal discord, and "Sun Mouth" formations as indicators of treacherous individuals or high-ranking plots to seize power.</summary>
<keywords>Crossed Vapor, Sun Mouth, solar divination, military conflict, internal rebellion, treason, political instability</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...They are bright but not dazzling. Being gentle and compliant, they nurture all categories of things <gloss>categories refers to objects</gloss>. Their virtue encompasses the foolish and tolerates the unworthy, with no selfish preference <gloss>selfish refers to deviance</gloss>. Those who employ the six pitch-pipes <note>referring to the system of twelve musical pitches used to regulate the calendar and administrative standards</note> suppress chaos and forbid violence, promote the worthy and dismiss the unworthy, and support the faltering to establish order <gloss>support and faltering refers to duty and administration</gloss>. They collapse the dangerous to make it level and straighten the crooked to make it true <gloss>correcting that which is crooked and bent</gloss>. They are enlightened regarding the principles of prohibition and granting, opening and closing, and they ride the timing and rely upon circumstances to command the hearts of the people <gloss>command refers to service and employment</gloss>.

Those who claim the title of Emperor imitate Yin and Yang, yet are invaded <gloss>invaded refers to being encroached upon and bullied by the various Xia states</gloss>. Those who are Kings model themselves on the Four Seasons, yet are diminished <gloss>diminished refers to having territory whittled away by the various Xia states</gloss>. Those who are Hegemons regulate the six pitch-pipes, yet are shamed <gloss>shamed refers to being insulted by neighboring states</gloss>. Those who are Lords lose the level and the plumb line, and are deposed <gloss>deposed refers to being dismissed and replaced by ministers with a worthy ruler</gloss>. Therefore, to be small but act large results in being unrefined and unapproachable <gloss>unrefined means not full or dense; unapproachable means not cherished or attached to by ministers and subordinates</gloss>. To be large but act small results in being cramped and unable to contain others <gloss>acting small results in policies that are cramped and unable to encompass one's subordinates</gloss>. When the noble and the humble do not lose their proper station, the world is at peace.

<summary>This passage contrasts the ideal administration of a sage-ruler with the failures of lesser leaders, emphasizing the necessity of moral alignment with natural principles like Yin-Yang and the seasonal cycles to maintain political stability.</summary>
<keywords>Huainanzi, Yin-Yang, Six Pitch-Pipes, Sage-ruler, Governance, Political Philosophy</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: They are broad but not loose, and they are solemn but not contrary.</meta> They are gentle, flexible, and compliant in order to nurture the myriad classes of things <gloss>classes means things</gloss>. Their virtue encompasses the simple and tolerates the unworthy; they have no partiality or favoritism <gloss>partiality refers to selfishness</gloss>. Those who use the six pitch-pipes <note>The six pitch-pipes refer to the traditional Chinese musical tuning system, used here as a metaphor for setting standards and maintaining administrative order.</note> strike down disorder and curb violence, promote the worthy and dismiss the unworthy, and support the faltering to establish what is correct <gloss>supporting the faltering means appointing and governing</gloss>. They break down dangerous barriers to establish equality and correct what is crooked to make it straight <gloss>correcting means fixing the crooked and bent</gloss>. They are enlightened regarding the principles of prohibitions, permissions, openings, and closings; they ride the times and leverage circumstances to utilize the hearts of the people <gloss>utilizing means to employ</gloss>. If an Emperor <note>An Emperor (Ti) represents the highest form of enlightened rule based on natural principles.</note> embodies Yin and Yang, they will be encroached upon <gloss>encroached means to be invaded or bullied by the various Xia states</gloss>. If a King <note>A King (Wang) represents a ruler who governs through benevolence and standard social structures.</note> models themselves on the Four Seasons, they will be whittled down <gloss>whittled means to be reduced or diminished by the various Xia states</gloss>. If a Hegemon <note>A Hegemon (Ba) is a ruler who relies on force and alliances rather than absolute virtue.</note> regulates themselves by the six pitch-pipes, they will be humiliated <gloss>humiliated means to be insulted by neighboring states</gloss>. If a Ruler <note>A Ruler (Jun) is a general term for a sovereign.</note> loses the balance scale and the plumb line, they will be deposed <gloss>deposed means to be cast aside by ministers and replaced with a worthy successor</gloss>. Therefore, if one is small but attempts to execute great acts, they will be disconnected and lacking intimacy <gloss>disconnected means not fully satisfying the close relations; lacking intimacy means not being supported or attached to by subjects</gloss>. If one is great but attempts to execute small acts, they will be cramped and constrained, unable to hold others <gloss>executing small acts means governance is cramped and constrained, unable to contain or accommodate subordinates</gloss>. When the high and low do not lose their proper nature, the world acts as one.

<summary>This passage discusses the relationship between a ruler's governance style and the natural consequences of their methods. It categorizes different types of rulers, such as Emperors and Hegemons, and explains that failing to align with the appropriate natural standards, such as Yin and Yang or the Four Seasons, leads to political instability and failure.</summary>
<keywords>Governance, Emperor, Hegemon, Yin and Yang, Six Pitch-Pipes, Virtue, Political Order</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...the complete revealing of the truths of what was foretold by the symbols of the revealed laws regarding the Seal [of Prophets], and stripping them of the garments of forms entirely, is deferred from his time. It only appears in the genesis of the one who is the <term>Paraclete</term> <gloss>the Comforter/Helper</gloss> and the manifestation of his specific sainthood.</meta>

If [the truth] is revealed, it is because the Seal-prophecy in its essence is in the most complete state within the genesis of Prophecy, such that <margin>he reached the station of...</margin> its <unclear>glory</unclear> <margin>its exaltation</margin> folded <margin>its excellence</margin> into its naming, and no forms remained upon it. For the Truth has subtle realities that manifest in, and the <unclear>remnant</unclear> of those realities is the beauty of those Truths. Therefore, the <term>Paraclete</term> said all the prophets and the <unclear>disclosing</unclear> <margin>from</margin> realities of their prophets, but some of those manifestations remained. So, your understanding is that the requirement of Prophecy is paused and entrusted to the revealing of <insert>to there</insert> the manifestations of his specific sainthood, in consideration of what is appropriate for the readiness of the time. There is no doubt that the lights of the <term>Kingdom</term> <gloss>Malakut</gloss> are descending without an end to the <unclear>perceivers</unclear>, <margin>no end of</margin> and there is no restriction in them. The ray of the Sacred spreads over the prepared, detached souls. The path of Truth opens for whoever knocks at its door, meaning that the door of God is open. For the Bestower of Knowledge, who is at the High Horizon, the One who is not miserly regarding the Unseen, therein flash meanings of a rank such that it is hidden from one who possesses discernment. As the Guardians of the brilliant, preserved light informed, its action in the language comes from "preservation" in the sense of seizing. The intended meaning here is a subtle hidden-ness from the world of the senses.

The extinguishing of lights is evanescent, not stable, and it follows a flashing light <margin>the overflowing of</margin> upon the soul on the night of the "sleeping of the <term>Nawwuj</term>" <gloss>the storm-winds</gloss>. This is in the language, the violent wind that uproots houses. The intended meaning here is the hardship leading to the rejection of bodily powers. This is not achieved except by the blowing of the winds of attraction from the Higher Ascent, as he, peace be upon him, said: "Glad tidings to whoever sends the winds as heralds before his mercy." And the easy [way] is in his hand, meaning the hour of its owner, meaning the owner of preservation, descending; and it is a <unclear>luminous</unclear> <term>nur</term> <gloss>light</gloss> from him, ascending from him as a form of that witnessing.

<summary>This passage continues the discussion of the Paraclete as the manifestation of the final and complete phase of prophecy, explaining how the truths of earlier prophetic symbols are revealed through the sainthood of the Seal of Prophets. It further describes the spiritual states of detachment and the descent of divine light as necessary for the unveiling of hidden realities.</summary>

<keywords>Paraclete, Seal of Prophets, Sainthood, Malakut, spiritual illumination, Divine Knowledge, unveiling</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: the complete revealing of the truths of what was foretold by the symbols of the revealed laws is</meta> on the seal, and stripping it of the garments of forms entirely, delayed from its time. For it only appears in the station of the one who is the <term>Paraclete</term> <gloss>the Comforter/Helper</gloss> and the manifestation of his specific sainthood. And if he revealed [the truth], it is because the Final Prophecy <note>referring to the prophethood of Muhammad</note> itself is at its most perfect in the station of prophecy, such that it is folded <margin>it attained</margin> <margin>its name was elevated</margin> <margin>it contains/encompasses</margin> within its essence. Nothing remained upon it of the forms, and for the Truth are delicate realities that manifest in the remainder. 

From these [remain] the beauty of those Truths. That is why the <term>Paraclete</term> said all the prophets and the <unclear>gatherer</unclear> <margin>from</margin> are the realities of their prophets, but some of those manifestations remained. So he [the Prophet] addresses you with the requirement of prophecy, [which is] suspended and entrusted to his revealing <insert>to there</insert> the manifestations of his specific sainthood, observing what is appropriate for the readiness of the time. There is no doubt that the Lights of the Kingdom <note>divine realm</note> are descending, with no limit to the perceivers, and no prevention <margin>no limit</margin> in them. The Ray of Holiness spreads upon the prepared, detached souls, and the path of the Truth opens to those who knock at its door. This means that the door of God is open, for the Bestower of Knowledge, who is at the Highest Horizon, is not stingy with the Unseen. In it, [meanings] shimmer with a rank, for it has [a quality] like the Most Hidden <note>a reference to a specific Sufi rank of consciousness</note> to the discerning one, just as the guards of the preserved brilliance informed [us]. 

In the language, its action is from "preservation" <note>Arabic: hifz</note>, meaning extraction. The intended meaning here is a subtle Unseen, away from the world of the senses. The vanishing of the lights is not constant; it follows a flashing light <margin>the overflow of the unseen</margin> upon the soul on the night of the "uprooting" <note>Arabic: nawuja</note>, which in the language is the violent wind that uproots houses. The intention here is the discipline that leads to the rejection of the physical powers. This is not achieved except by the blowing of the winds of attractions from the Highest Source, as he, peace be upon him, said: "Glad tidings to he who sends the winds as heralds before His mercy." The ease is the [gentle] hand <unclear>in it</unclear>, meaning the hour of its master, meaning the master of the preservation, descending, and the "model" <note>Arabic: mūd</note> of the light is ascending from it, [as is] the form of that witnessing.

<summary>This page discusses the nature of the Paraclete as the manifestation of the Final Prophecy, the role of divine illumination in the "Highest Horizon," and the metaphor of "uprooting" as a spiritual discipline for stripping away physical attachments.</summary>
<keywords>Paraclete, Final Prophecy, Lights of the Kingdom, Ray of Holiness, Highest Horizon, spiritual discipline, manifestation</keywords>

...upon the seal and stripping it of the garments of forms entirely, delaying from its time, for it only appears in the emergence of the one who is the <term>Paraclete</term> <gloss>comforter or messenger</gloss> and the manifestation of his specific sainthood. Even if it is unveiled, because <term>seal-prophecy</term> <gloss>the final prophecy</gloss> itself is in the most complete state within the emergence of prophecy, such that it is folded within its brilliance. It <note>referring to the seal</note> was upon its symbolic naming, and no forms remained upon it. For the Truth has subtle essences that manifest in, and the remainder of them is the beauty of those Truths. Therefore, the <term>Paraclete</term> said all the prophets and the uncovering are truths of their prophets, but some of those manifestations remained. Thus, the requirements of prophecy are suspended, entrusted to the unveiling of the manifestations of his specific sainthood, observing what is appropriate for the readiness of the time. There is no doubt that the <term>lights of the kingdom</term> <gloss>divine realms</gloss> are descending, not having a limit for those who touch them, with no prevention in them, and that the <term>ray of the holy</term> <gloss>divine radiation</gloss> spreads upon the prepared, detached souls. The path of Truth opens for those who knock at its door, meaning that the door of God is open. For the <term>Bestower of Knowledge</term> <gloss>God</gloss>, who is at the <term>highest horizon</term> <gloss>the ultimate cosmic boundary</gloss>, is not stingy with the unseen. In it, meanings appear with a rank, as if it is more hidden to the possessor of intelligence, just as the <term>Preserved Tablet</term> <gloss>the divine register</gloss> has informed us. "Preserved" in language: its verb is from "hifz," meaning to snatch away. The intended meaning here is a subtle unseen from the <term>world of the senses</term> <gloss>the manifest, physical realm</gloss>. <note>The</note> extinguished lights are unsteady, not fixed, following a flashing light upon the soul on the night of the "al-Nu'uj" <note>a metaphorical storm or tempest</note>. It is in the language the violent wind that uproots houses. The intended meaning here is the hardship leading to the rejection of bodily powers, and that is not achieved except by the blowing of the winds of attractions from the highest source, as he, peace be upon him, said: "Glad tidings to whoever sends the winds as a herald before His mercy." The easy path—he is in it, meaning a moment from its owner, meaning the owner of the preservation, descending, and in him is the return from the light, ascending from him the image of that witnessing.

<summary>This passage discusses the nature of the Paraclete as the manifestation of final prophecy and specific sainthood, emphasizing the transition from physical forms to the unveiling of divine truths through spiritual receptivity.</summary>
<keywords>Paraclete, seal-prophecy, lights of the kingdom, highest horizon, world of the senses, divine knowledge</keywords>

pages.299:
<meta>continues from previous page: ...the <term>‘afwah</term> <gloss>the healing process</gloss> and the healing process is below it or not flat at the bottom. Likewise, the hand and palm and others have been attached; the healing process always attaches downwards.</meta>

This is what he says. He also says: Sometimes a wound occurs where it requires complete amputation. Regarding the limb, if the wound has resulted in amputation of a part of it, and it is large, it requires flesh-regenerating agents. What dries and prevents <note>prevents the accumulation of pus or excess moisture</note> is not enough; rather, sometimes the dryer and the preventer, in a certain respect, hinder the matter from which it grows. Sometimes there is a depth and a deficit in the bone such that it cannot grow completely, so a depression remains, as in a condition where it may happen that it grows more than is necessary, resulting in excessive flesh. It is necessary for the patient who wants to grow flesh in a wound to avoid excessive movement. The regenerating agent may be such that it is possible for the flesh to grow. As for the skin, because if it has been completely severed, it does not grow in its place; rather, firm flesh grows in its place, upon which no hair or veins grow. However, branches are generated and it grows like flesh. Among the wounds are those that are dangerous, such as the wounds occurring in the nerves and the muscles of the upper arm, and we will mention this in the chapter on nerves. Often, hideous and bad symptoms follow them. The worst thing that follows a wound to the area of the upper arm is a change in color and the dropping of the pulse, followed by a trace and shrinking, leading to emaciation and a loss of strength. Convulsions may also follow it. Likewise, those that occur in front of the knee at the patella; for they are followed by bad symptoms, and they are fatal, rarely being relieved. And if a convulsion occurs from such upper arm wounds and the treatment does not heal, the treatment is the amputation of the upper arm, and satisfaction.

<summary>This passage discusses the management of deep wounds and the complications arising from nerve or muscle damage, particularly in the limbs. It details the challenges of flesh regeneration, the risk of tissue loss, and the severe, often fatal, symptoms such as convulsions that necessitate amputation in extreme cases.</summary>
<keywords>wounds, flesh regeneration, nerve damage, muscle injury, amputation, clinical treatment, Avicenna, Canon of Medicine</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...the <term>‘afwah</term> <gloss>the healing process</gloss> below it or otherwise positioned at the bottom. The hand, the palm, and other parts are also suspended, for the <term>‘afwah</term> <gloss>the healing process</gloss> always hangs downward.</meta>

This is his statement. He also says that a wound may occur where it requires a complete amputation. Regarding the limb, if the wound requires an amputation of part of it, it does not become excessive, so it requires agents for the regeneration of flesh. It is not sufficient to merely use things that dry and prevent [matter], but rather, the drying and preventing agent might, in some respects, stimulate the matter from which it grows. Sometimes there is a depression and deficiency in the bone such that it cannot fully grow, leaving a cavity. A situation may occur where more than the necessary amount grows, resulting in proud flesh <note>original: "لحم زائد", referring to hypergranulation tissue</note>. It is necessary for the patient to be moderate, as the intention is to grow flesh in a wound without excessive, unnecessary growth. The regenerating agent might be such that it allows the flesh to grow. 

As for the skin, because if it is completely severed, it does not grow back in its place; rather, firm flesh grows in its place, upon which neither hair nor veins grow. Instead, branches are generated, and it grows like flesh. Among the wounds are those that are dangerous, specifically wounds that occur in the nerves and the muscles of the upper arm, and we will mention this in the chapter on nerves. Often, hideous and severe symptoms follow them. The worst thing that follows a wound to the tip of the upper arm is a change in color, the cessation of the pulse afterward, and the smallness and weakness that leads to fainting and the collapse of strength. Convulsions may also follow it. Likewise, those that occur in front of the knee at the kneecap, for they are followed by severe symptoms, and they are lasting and rarely recover from them. If convulsions occur from such wounds of the upper arm and the treatment does not heal, the treatment is the amputation of the upper arm, and [this is] the last resort.

<summary>This page discusses the surgical treatment of deep wounds, the management of flesh regeneration, the avoidance of hypergranulation, and the grave risks associated with nerve and muscle wounds in the limbs, which can lead to convulsions or necessitate amputation.</summary>
<keywords>Canon of Medicine, Avicenna, surgery, wound management, flesh regeneration, nerve damage, convulsions, amputation</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta> and the healing process <note>original: "al-‘afwah"</note> is below it, or it is not positioned at the bottom. Likewise, the hand, the palm, and others always have the healing process oriented downward.

Thus, this is his statement. He says: Sometimes the wound occurs where it requires you to perform a complete amputation. As for the limb, if the wound has caused a large amount of tissue loss, it requires flesh-regenerating agents. It is not enough to use what dries and inhibits; rather, the drying and inhibiting agent sometimes blocks the material from which the flesh grows. The depression and loss in the bone may be such that it cannot fully regenerate, so a depression remains, as in a condition that may occur where more than the necessary amount grows, resulting in *proud flesh* <note>excessive granulation tissue</note>. The patient whose flesh one intends to regenerate in a wound must be monitored without this, for good regeneration may be such that it allows the flesh to grow. As for the skin, because if it has been completely severed, flesh grows in its place that is hard and upon which hair and veins do not grow, though branches form and it grows like flesh.

Among the wounds are dangerous wounds: the wounds that occur in the nerves and the muscles of the arm, and we will mention this in the chapter on nerves, and the symptoms that follow them are abominable and bad. The worst of what follows a wound to the tip of the arm is a change in color and the disappearance of the pulse after it, followed by shrinkage, leading to fainting and a collapse of strength. Convulsions may also follow it. Likewise, those that occur in front of the knee at the kneecap, for they are followed by bad symptoms, and they are usually such that they rarely recover from them. And if a convulsion occurs from such brachial <note>arm-related</note> wounds and the treatment does not heal it, the treatment is the amputation of the arm, and God knows best.

<summary>This passage discusses the management of deep wounds, the necessity of flesh-regenerating agents versus drying agents, and the treatment of severe wounds involving nerves and muscles in the arm and knee.</summary>
<keywords>wound management, flesh regeneration, proud flesh, nerve wounds, amputation, surgery</keywords>

...Zalim <term>Ismah</term> <gloss>the immunity or protection of the oppressed</gloss> by enslavement, then it was confirmed. <term>Ali ibn Isa ibn Mahan</term> set out for <term>Khorasan</term>, for he had released him. When <term>al-Ma'mun</term> heard of this, he dispatched <term>Tahir ibn al-Husayn ibn Mus'ab al-Bushanji</term> from <term>Merv</term> with four thousand men. He met <term>Ali ibn Isa</term> at <term>al-Rayy</term> and killed him. Then, <term>al-Ma'mun</term> also sent <term>Harthama ibn A'yan</term> to <term>Iraq</term>. <term>al-Ma'mun</term> remained in <term>Merv</term> until <term>Muhammad</term> <note>refers to the Caliph al-Amin</note> was killed at the end of <term>Muharram</term> in the year one hundred and ninety-eight, and allegiance was sworn to him <note>al-Ma'mun</note> as Caliph. 

Then <term>al-Ma'mun</term> remained in <term>Khorasan</term> during the year one hundred and ninety-nine and the year two hundred, while he continued to send men to <term>Iraq</term>. He sent <term>Humayd ibn Abd al-Hamid ibn Rib'i al-Ta'i al-Tusi</term>, then he sent <term>Ali ibn Hisham ibn Khusraw al-Marwazi</term>. Then he sent the one with two banners <note>a title of honor</note>, <term>al-Hasan ibn Abi Sa'id ibn Khallad</term>, then <term>al-Fadl ibn Sahl</term> over the land tax of <term>Iraq</term>, and then he sent <term>al-Hasan ibn Sahl</term> over all affairs. <term>Harthama</term> returned from <term>Iraq</term> in anger and came to <term>al-Ma'mun</term>, who imprisoned him. He died in prison three days later in <term>Merv</term> in the year two hundred. 

Then <term>al-Ma'mun</term> took the oath of allegiance for <term>al-Rida</term>, <term>Ali ibn Musa ibn Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib</term> <note>the eighth Imam of the Shi'a</note>, in <term>Merv</term> as successor to the throne in the year two hundred and two. The poetic tradition of the Eastern Kingdom <note>refers to Korea</note> differs from that of the Central Kingdom <note>refers to China</note>. In the Central Kingdom, the trends of the times flow daily toward elaborate craftsmanship and excessive refinement. The Eastern Kingdom still values ancient methods. Even when the rhythm is not perfectly harmonious or word choice is forced, the innate naturalness remains, which does not diminish its excellence. In the Gyeongja year <note>1800</note>, I met with the brothers Yi Sun-gye and Niam to discuss this in a book. Now,

Puwon has brought this piece to show me. Its sentiments are transcendental and expansive. It is what one would call a work where the spirit emerges in ancient and extraordinary ways, revealing a marvelous aesthetic. At times it shows a crisp and refreshing style, sufficient to startle the eye, and one knows that what it contains is not of the ordinary world. How could one not be moved? The rise of Puwon is different from the common run of men. If Lu has no noble men <note>a reference to the Analects, questioning where one finds such virtue if not among the learned</note>, where else would one take them from? Truly, how many virtuous men the Eastern Kingdom possesses! Unrolling this scroll, I cannot bear to let it go. It is indeed as the saying goes: reading new poetry until the blue mountains grow dark. However, expressions like "floating clouds and tree colors," "Jialing's heart at sunset," and "river sounds in the autumn" evoke the breadth of Master Yu <note>Yu Ji, a renowned Yuan dynasty scholar</note>. The frost of the fifth watch enters one's clothes, autumn is born in the Yu Garden, the chickens return while the guest is few, and arriving at the high tower, one speaks of many things, ashamed of the stillness of the pavilion, unable to match the heights of the peaks in the slightest.

<summary>A critique of Korean poetry, praising its natural, archaic quality in contrast to the over-refined trends of contemporary Chinese verse, followed by an appreciation of the poet Puwon's work.</summary>
<keywords>Eastern Kingdom, poetic tradition, Puwon, Yi Sun-gye, Niam, literary critique, aesthetic naturalness</keywords>

<header>[ The Excellence of Geomancy ]</header>

Once you have determined the nature of the <term>Kharij</term> <gloss>Outgoing</gloss> and other figures, you should explain the result of the querent's <term>Nirgam</term> <gloss>Outgoing/Departure</gloss> question to them, stating whether it will result in auspicious or inauspicious outcomes, and whether it will be achieved through ease or great labor. ॥ १७ ॥ Having carefully considered all such questions regarding departure and similar matters, present them to the querent. In this process, success in divination is achieved only when the <term>Rammal</term> <gloss>practitioner of geomancy</gloss> maintains a steady mind, has faith in the <term>Ramal-shastra</term> <gloss>science of geomancy</gloss> and the teacher, and possesses purity of heart. ॥ १८ ॥

->Thus concludes the method for departure and related matters.<-

->Now, the purpose of the <term>Inkilab</term> <gloss>Transmutation/Change</gloss> question.<-

Now I shall speak of the results arising from questions regarding <term>Inkilab</term>. If a <term>Jamaat</term> <gloss>congregation/assemblage of figures</gloss> occurs in the fifteenth house on that date, one should declare the outcome based on its roots. ॥ १९ ॥ If the figures in the thirteenth and fourteenth houses are <term>Kharij</term> and are known as <term>Vishvashakra</term> <gloss>all-powerful</gloss>, and if they are Auspicious, they provide success in a <term>Nirgam</term> <gloss>departure</gloss> question. If they are <term>Dakhil</term> <gloss>Incoming</gloss> and Auspicious, they grant success just as in an <term>Agam</term> <gloss>arrival</gloss> question. ॥ २० ॥ If they are <term>Savite</term> <gloss>Fixed/Stable</gloss> and Auspicious, they grant success for firm and lasting work. Success is moderate if the figures are of medium strength, and success is slight if they are weak. ॥ २१ ॥ The result is reversed if the figures are inauspicious, just as before. Having considered everything, one should speak to the querent, as the analysis of the question remains the same as previously described. ॥ २२ ॥ Questions regarding the fist, the silent, and the duration of a question, among others, are considered successful without the need for <term>Inkilab</term>; therefore, <term>Inkilab</term> does not apply to these. ॥ २३ ॥ Thus, the determination for all houses has been spoken of in general. Now, I shall speak of the specific details for each house. ॥ २४ ॥

**Commentary**—Now, the purpose of the <term>Inkilab</term> is explained: in this context, if a <term>Jamaat</term> is formed in the fifteenth house from the question arising through <term>Inkilab</term>, one should declare the result based on its roots in the thirteenth and fourteenth houses. ॥ १९ ॥ It is thus: if the figures in the thirteenth and fourteenth houses are <term>Kharij</term> and Auspicious, they provide success for a <term>Nirgam</term> question. If they are <term>Dakhil</term> and Auspicious, they provide success for an <term>Agam</term> question.

<summary>This page concludes the guidelines for "Departure" questions and introduces the "Transmutation" (Inkilab) category, detailing how house-based root calculations influence the outcome of the divination.</summary>
<keywords>Nirgam, Inkilab, Jamaat, Kharij, Dakhil, Savite, geomantic houses, divination methodology</keywords>

<page-num>58</page-num>
<header>[ The Gem of Ramal ]</header>

Determine whether the <term>Kharij</term> <gloss>Outgoing</gloss> and other figures are auspicious or inauspicious. Having decided this, state the result of the querent's <term>Nirgam</term> <gloss>Outgoing/Departure</gloss> clearly, whether it will come through ease or great labor. ॥ 17 ॥ In this way, after considering the <term>Nirgam</term> and all such questions, one should present them to the querent. In this process, if the <term>Rammal</term> <gloss>geomancer</gloss> maintains a steady focus, faith in the <term>Ramal-shastra</term> <gloss>science of geomancy</gloss> and the teacher, and possesses purity of heart, then the success of the question is assured. ॥ 18 ॥

->Thus concludes the method of <term>Nirgam</term> and related procedures.<-

->Now, the purpose of <term>Inkilab</term> <gloss>Change/Transformation</gloss>.<-

Now I speak of the result arising from a question regarding <term>Inkilab</term>. If a <term>Jama</term> <gloss>Congregation</gloss> occurs in the fifteenth house, one should declare the result based on the roots of that house (houses 13 and 14). ॥ 19 ॥ If the figures in houses 13 and 14 are <term>Kharij</term> and <term>Vishvashakra</term> <gloss>a specific auspicious configuration</gloss>, they are auspicious and provide success in a <term>Nirgam</term> question. If they are <term>Dakhil</term> <gloss>Incoming</gloss> and auspicious, they signify the success of an <term>Agam</term> <gloss>Incoming/Arrival</gloss> question. ॥ 20 ॥ If they are <term>Savite</term> <gloss>Fixed/Stable</gloss> and auspicious, they likewise provide success in a stable task. With moderate strength, there is moderate success, and with weakness, there is little success. ॥ 21 ॥ The result is inverted if the figures are inauspicious, just as stated previously. Having considered all this, one should explain the entire question segment as described before. ॥ 22 ॥ Questions regarding <term>Mushti</term> <gloss>Fist/Hidden</gloss>, <term>Muka</term> <gloss>Silent</gloss>, and <term>Shar</term> <gloss>Arrow/Shot</gloss> <note>these refer to specific methods of random selection or 'casting' of the figures</note>—these are considered successful without needing <term>Inkilab</term>; therefore, <term>Inkilab</term> does not apply to these. ॥ 23 ॥ Thus, the decision-making process for all houses has been stated generally. Now, I shall explain the specific results for each house individually. ॥ 24 ॥

**Commentary—** Now, the purpose of <term>Inkilab</term> is explained. If a <term>Jama</term> occurs in the 15th house for a question arising from <term>Inkilab</term> at this time, the result should be spoken based on its roots, houses 13 and 14. ॥ 19 ॥ This is because if the figures from 13 and 14 are <term>Kharij</term> and auspicious, they grant success for an <term>Nirgam</term> question. If they are <term>Dakhil</term> and auspicious, they grant success for an <term>Agam</term> question.

<summary>This page explains the role of "Inkilab" or transformational figures in geomantic readings, focusing on the 15th house and its roots (13 and 14) to determine the success of specific types of questions, while also noting exceptions for "hidden" or "silent" question methods.</summary>
<keywords>Inkilab, Nirgam, Agam, Kharij, Dakhil, Jama, 15th house, geomantic rules</keywords>

<page-num>५८</page-num>
<header>[ Ramal-Param ]</header>

Having ascertained the nature of the <term>Kharij</term> <gloss>Outgoing</gloss> and other figures, one should speak of the result regarding the querent's departure, whether it will be auspicious or inauspicious, or whether it will be achieved through effort. ॥ ۱۷ ॥ In this way, after considering the departure and all such questions, one should present the conclusion to the querent. In this, the practitioner’s <term>Rammal</term> <gloss>geomancer's</gloss> mental focus must be stable, and there must be faith in the <term>Ramal-shastra</term> <gloss>science of geomancy</gloss> and the <term>Guru</term> <gloss>teacher</gloss>. When the mind is purified, the question achieves success. ॥ ۱۸ ॥

->Thus ends the section on the method of departure.<-

->Now, the purpose of <term>Inkilab</term> <gloss>transformation/reversal</gloss> begins.<-

Now I shall speak of the fruits arising from the <term>Inkilab</term> <gloss>transformation</gloss> question. If there is a <term>Jama</term> <gloss>gathering/junction</gloss> in the <note>fifteenth</note> house, one should speak the result from its roots. ॥ ۱۹ ॥ When there is a <term>Kharij</term> <gloss>Outgoing</gloss> in the <term>Vishva-shakra</term> <gloss>a specific house or formation</gloss>, and the <term>Nirgam</term> <gloss>departure</gloss> is auspicious, it grants success. If there is a <term>Dakhil</term> <gloss>Incoming</gloss> and it is auspicious, it acts like a coming and grants success. ॥ ۲۰ ॥ Similarly, if a <term>Savite</term> <gloss>fixed/stable figure</gloss> is auspicious, it grants the success of a firm task. If it is of medium strength, there is success, and if it is weak, there is only minor success. ॥ ۲۱ ॥ If there is a reversal, success will occur as before, just as with the auspicious and other types. One should consider all these things and speak on the entire question, as previously described. ॥ ۲۲ ॥ <term>Mushti</term> <gloss>fist/hand-based divination</gloss>, <term>Muka</term> <gloss>silent</gloss>, and <term>Sharu</term> <gloss>arrow/start-based</gloss> methods, along with the <term>Avadhi-prashna-hara</term> <gloss>the named type of time-limit question</gloss>, are successful even without <term>Inkilab</term> <gloss>transformation</gloss>; therefore, it does not apply to these. ॥ ۲۳ ॥ In this way, the judgment for all houses has been stated generally. Now, I shall describe the specific effects for each house. ॥ ۲۴ ॥

**Commentary—** Now, we state the purpose of <term>Inkilab</term> <gloss>transformation</gloss>. It is said that at this time, regarding a question generated by <term>Inkilab</term>, if there is a <term>Jama</term> <gloss>gathering</gloss> in the 15th house, one should predict the result from its roots in the 13th and 14th houses. ॥ ۱۹ ॥ It is as follows: if the figures in the 13th and 14th houses are <term>Kharij</term> <gloss>Outgoing</gloss> and auspicious, they grant success for a <term>Nirgam</term> <gloss>departure</gloss> question. If they are <term>Dakhil</term> <gloss>Incoming</gloss> and auspicious, they grant success for an <term>Agam</term> <gloss>arrival</gloss> question.

<summary>This page explains the role of "Inkilab" or transformation figures in geomancy, detailing how specific configurations in the houses (particularly the 13th, 14th, and 15th) indicate the success or failure of departure and arrival questions. It also differentiates between various divination methods like Mushti and the standard geomantic inquiry.</summary>
<keywords>Inkilab, Kharij, Dakhil, Jama, Nirgam, Agam, Savite, Geomantic houses, Divination methods</keywords>

The dust is seen rising in advance of us; the chariot of you, who hold the reins, although it has descended to the earth, is not seen to have done so by reason of its not touching the surface of the ground. *Upodha-śabdāḥ* means "having reached a sound," according to the commentator (compare *upodha-rāga* in Act II of the *Vikramorvaśīyam*). *Pravartamāna* may mean "rising in front of us." *Nirundhatāḥ* means "holding back." *Na lakshyate* means "is not perceived." In the *Vikramorvaśīyam*, Act I, when the chariot of Purūravas touches the ground, the stage direction is *rathāvatāra-kṣobham nāṭayantī*, "acting the concussion caused by the descent of the chariot." Such, Mātali remarks, is the difference between the chariot of Indra and that of mortal heroes.

1 "Where stands yon sage, facing the sun’s orb, immovable as the trunk of a tree, his body half-buried in an ant-hill, his chest closely encircled by a snake’s skin, his throat excessively pinched by a necklace formed of the tendril of a withered creeper, wearing a circular mass of matted hair enveloping his shoulders and filled with birds' nests." *Valmīkārdha*, and so on, is the reading of the commentator and the Mackenzie manuscript; the other Devanagari manuscripts read *valmīkāgra*. *Valmīka* (a heap of earth made by ants) is the mound of earth thrown up by the large ants of India. These hillocks sometimes rise, in Bengal, to the height of eight or ten feet, and are held sacred (see Manu 4.46, 238). Such was the immovable impassiveness of this ascetic that the ants had thrown up their mound as high as his waist without being disturbed, and the birds had built their nests in his hair. *Sandaṣṭa-s°* means "embraced by a cast-off skin"; compare page 120, note 3. <meta>continues from previous page: ...The unfulfilled purpose of the puruṣa is the cause of existence for the mind, which has arisen from its own cause. It provides an example: "Just as for the body," etc.</meta>

As light is to form, so is the perception of form; it is the cause of modification, another object for the mind. As fire is to that which is to be cooked. The cause of perception is the knowledge of smoke for the knowledge of fire. The cause of attainment is the practice of the limbs of Yoga for discriminative discernment.
The cause of separation is that same practice for impurity. The cause of differentiation is, for example, a goldsmith for gold. Thus, in the case of a single perception of a woman, ignorance is the cause of delusion, while aversion is the cause of suffering.

<column-break/>

Through the senses or by itself, the manifestation of the transformation of an object—its cause is like light for form. The cause of modification is another object for the mind. For instance, consider the man whose mind was composed, yet who, immediately upon hearing the fifth note played on a lute <note>original: "vallakī"</note>, opened his eyes and gazed upon the nymph Pramlocā, who was endowed with beauty and youth; he abandoned his concentration (<term>samādhi</term>) and his mind became attached to her. Here, the text provides an illustration: **"As fire is to that which is to be cooked,"** <note>referring to rice, etc., which possesses a structure of hard components; fire is the cause of its modification, defined as the loosening of the combination of its parts.</note> So too, the knowledge of smoke is the cause of the perception of fire, for an object that already exists. "Knowledge" (<term>jñāna</term>) means that which is known; "fire" is the known and "knowledge" is the perception, so this refers to the knowledge of fire. This is what is meant: the fire, which is already present as an object to be known, serves as the cause because it is the object that produces the perception. By nature, the causal efficacy of causes that are not obstructed results in the attainment of their effect; the exception to this, where attainment does not occur, is due to some hindrance. Just as the flow of water, which naturally tends to move downward, is blocked by a dam, here too, the intellect (<term>buddhi-sattva</term>), which is of the nature of happiness and luminosity, naturally tends to generate discriminative discernment. That generation does not occur due to some obstruction, such as demerit (<term>dharma</term>) or darkness (<term>tamas</term>). Upon the removal of that obstruction through merit or the practice of the limbs of Yoga, the intellect attains the capacity to generate that discernment, purely by virtue of its own unobstructed nature. As the text will say: "The cause is not the activator of the creative sources; rather, it is the removal of the barrier, like a farmer."

Thus, the "cause of attainment" has been stated with regard to the effect characterized as discriminative discernment. With regard to an intermediate effect, it says that the same is the "cause of separation." It states the "cause of differentiation": just as a goldsmith is to gold. Gold, which is distinct or non-distinct from bracelets, necklaces, and armlets, differs from a pendant depending on whether one wishes to focus on the distinction of form or the non-distinction of substance. Thus, the goldsmith, who creates something else from the gold—which is non-distinct from the pendant—is the cause of differentiation. Although fire is also the cause of differentiation for that which is being cooked, one cannot say there is differentiation in the substance, because when the two attributes (the state of being rice grains or rice mush) are not regarded as distinct, the substance persists even if its attributes appear and disappear. Therefore, it is stated to be merely the cause of modification, so there is no conflation of categories. It should not be explained that a change in configuration is the cause of a change in the substance, for that would make the example of the "goldsmith" incoherent. Having posited an external cause of differentiation, it illustrates an internal one: **"Thus, in the case of a single..."** Ignorance is the perception, such as "This woman is desirable," etc. Due to the association with delusion, that same perception of a woman...

Just as the knowledge of smoke is the cause of the knowledge of fire for an object that already exists. That which is known is knowledge, and that which is fire is also knowledge; thus, "knowledge of fire." This is what is meant—it is a cause because it is the cause of the perception of the fire that is the object to be known, which is already present. The attainment of the causal function of causes that are absolute and independent is natural; an exception to that, due to some factor, is non-attainment. Just as the flow of water, which has the nature of flowing downwards, is obstructed by a dam, so here too, the intellect-stuff (<term>buddhi-sattva</term>), which has the nature of pleasure and illumination, naturally has the capacity to generate discriminative realization. That does not occur due to some obstruction from demerit or darkness. Through merit, or through the practice of the limbs of Yoga, when that is removed, it attains that generating capacity due to the nature of its functioning being unobstructed. As it will say—the auxiliary cause is not the active producer of the primary causes, but it removes the barrier, like a farmer.

...through the senses or by itself, the manifestation of the object through processing is its cause, just as light is to form. [It is] the cause of the modification of the mind by another object.
