The knowledge of smoke is the cause of the perception of fire of an object that already exists. "Known" is knowledge, and that which is fire and is also knowledge is "fire-knowledge," of that. This is what is meant: the fire, which is the object of knowledge and is currently present, is the cause because it is the cause of the perception. The attainment of the action of an effect is the natural manifestation of causes that are not obstructed; the lack of attainment is the exception to this due to some cause. Just as a dam obstructs water, which has the nature of flowing downwards, so too here, for the <term>buddhi-sattva</term> <gloss>the essence of intelligence</gloss>, which has the nature of pleasure and illumination, the generation of discriminative knowledge of happiness is natural attainment. That does not occur due to some obstruction caused by merit or darkness. By the removal of that through the practice of the limbs of Yoga, the generation of that [knowledge] is attained by the very nature of an unobstructed flow. As it will say: "The cause is not the activator of the natures, but the removal of the obstruction occurs; it is like the farmer."

Thus, the cause of attainment is stated with respect to the effect characterized by discriminative knowledge. With respect to the intermediate effect, it is the cause of separation, which it states: "cause of separation." It states the cause of distinctness: "The cause of distinctness is like a goldsmith in relation to gold." Gold, which is different from a bracelet, earring, etc., when one wishes to express difference, is different from the bracelet; when one wishes to express non-difference, it is non-different from the bracelet. Thus, a goldsmith, a maker of bracelets, by making something different from the gold that is not different from the earring, is the cause of distinctness. The rule for arriving at the value of the cubical contents of an excavation, when the depth of the excavation varies (at various points), and also for arriving, when the cubical contents of an excavation are known, at the depth of digging necessary in the case of another (known) area (so that the cubical contents may be the same) :—

23½. The sum of the depths (measured in different places) is divided by the number of places; this gives rise to the (average) depth. The target, sixteen fingers wide and of equal height, should be made of iron, firm and resembling an elephant. <note>verse 44</note>
One should bind these firmly between two branches of a pillar, at the height of a man's chest. <note>verse 45</note>
Having pierced through them and emerged on the other side, the arrow should strike the ground; in this manner, one should practice hitting with skill. <note>verse 46</note>
When the arrow is held by the index finger at the side of the thumb, and the bow is held in the grip, with the nock properly positioned, this is called level-aiming. <note>verse 47</note>
In level-aiming, the string is drawn below; therefore, drawing from above is called upward-aiming. <note>verse 48</note>
Downward-aiming is appropriate for a target located high above, while upward-aiming is for a target located low below; for a target at eye level, it should be level. <note>verse 49</note>
A target sixteen fingers in circumference is called a coarse target, while one two fingers wide is fine, and one five fingers wide is a head-target. <note>verse 50</note>
A target inferred by sound is called a transcendent target; thus, the five types of targets should be demonstrated in their piercing. <note>verse 51</note>
Moving horizontally, going forward, rotating, and jumping up; their locations are said to be in the sky, on the ground, or in water. <note>verse 52</note>
Two hundred units is said to be the best distance, one hundred and fifty is the medium, and one hundred and twenty is the minimum for practice on the ground. <note>verse 53</note>
One should strike the best distance with four arrows at a slow pace, using arrows that are straight, thick, fine, or leaf-less. <note>verse 54</note>
The king should demonstrate agility by shooting one arrow in the fall, one in the hand, and five in the sky, thus practicing hitting the target. <note>verse 55</note>

**The Text of the Hymn is as follows—**

'To the Gayatri, to the Ushnih, to the Anushtup, to the Brihati, to the Pankti, to the Trishtup, to the Jagati' || 1 ||
Gayatri. Ushnih. Anushtup. Brihati. Pankti. Trishtup. Jagati || 1 ||

"Having assigned the verses among the seven meters, beginning with the Gayatri, in the manner of 'To the Gayatri, Svaha' <gloss>an offering invocation</gloss> and so on, according to the meter" (Shank 18,1). Because the method of modification <term>ūha</term> <gloss>adaptation of chants</gloss> for the mantras is shown there in the <term>Shantikalpa</term> <gloss>ritual manual for pacification</gloss>, there are seven mantras in this hymn: 'To the Gayatri, Svaha', 'To the Ushnih, Svaha', 'To the Anushtup, Svaha', 'To the Pankti, Svaha', 'To the Trishtup, Svaha', 'To the Jagati, Svaha'. All mantras are clear in their meaning.

**Thus ends the first hymn of the third anuvāka.**

The two hymns beginning with 'With the first of the Angirasas' are employed in the great pacification rite known as <term>Angirasi</term>, which is prescribed for one desiring sorcery and for one experiencing heavy rainfall (Shank 17,2). It is stated in the <term>Shantikalpa</term>: "A collection" (19,22:23) in the <term>Angirasi</term>. "O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts" (AV 2,5) in the <term>Aindri</term> <gloss>hymn dedicated to Indra</gloss> (Shank 18,1;4). Here, the word "collection" refers to these two hymns.

Therein, the hymn 'With the first of the Angirasas' is recited as follows—

**To the first of the Angirasas, to the five anuvākas, Svaha || 1 ||**
To the Angirasas. To the first. To the five. To the anuvākas. Svaha || 1 ||

**To the sixth, Svaha || 2 ||**
To the sixth. Svaha || 2 ||

**To the seventh and eighth, Svaha || 3 ||**
To the seventh and eighth. Svaha || 3 ||

**To the dark-colored ones, Svaha || 4 ||**
To the dark-colored ones. Svaha || 4 ||

**To the green ones, Svaha || 5 ||**
To the green ones. Svaha || 5 ||

**To the small ones, Svaha || 6 ||**
To the small ones. Svaha || 6 ||

**To the subsequent ones, Svaha || 7 ||**
To the subsequent ones. Svaha || 7 ||

**To the first empowered ones, Svaha || 8 ||**
To the first. To the empowered ones. Svaha || 8 ||

**To the second empowered ones, Svaha || 9 ||**
To the second. To the empowered ones. Svaha || 9 ||

**To the third empowered ones, Svaha || 10 ||**

"For the Gayatri, for the Ushnih, the Anushtup, the Brihati, the Pankti, the Trishtup, for the Jagati." || 1 ||
Gayatri. Ushnih. Anushtup. Brihati. Pankti. Trishtup. For the Jagati. || 1 ||

"Having fashioned the verses into seven meters, starting with the Gayatri, in accordance with the meter, such as 'To the Gayatri, Hail'." (Shaunaka 18.1). Because the method of adapting the mantras is shown there in the <term>Shantikalpa</term> <gloss>Rule of Pacification</gloss>, there are seven mantras in this hymn: "To the Gayatri, Hail," "To the Ushnih, Hail," "To the Anushtup, Hail," "To the Pankti, Hail," "To the Trishtup, Hail," "To the Jagati, Hail." All the mantras have clear meanings.

**Thus ends the first hymn of the third <term>anuvāka</term> <gloss>section</gloss>.**

The two hymns beginning with "To the first of the Angirasas" are employed in the great pacification rite known as <term>Angirasi</term>, which is prescribed in the <term>Shaunaka</term> text (17.2) for one who desires offspring and for one upon whom it is raining. It is said in the <term>Shantikalpa</term>: "The collection (19.22:23) is in the Angirasi. The 'Indra, attended by the Maruts' (Atharvaveda 2.5) is in the Aindra (rite)" (Shaunaka 18.1;4). Here, the word "collection" refers to these two hymns.

Regarding that, the hymn "To the first of the Angirasas" is handed down as follows:

**To the first of the Angirasas, for the five <term>anuvākas</term> <gloss>sections</gloss>, Hail. || 1 ||**

a small amount of that spark of life which animated, it is said, the pebbles of <term>Pyrrha</term> <note>a reference to the Greek myth where Pyrrha and Deucalion cast stones behind them to repopulate the earth</note>, I would make it my duty to repeat to him what I have just told you about Thales."

I replied to the man from Priene: "Mandraites, I conceive and share your enthusiasm; there is no danger except in the fanaticism of virtue and of truth. Go! Your account adds to the veneration I already held for the name of Thales. Your delirium is quite natural, and so is his. One does nothing great, one invents nothing sublime, if one does not possess the measure of one's own genius and the feeling of one's own strength. Thales is right to be jealous of his discovery; it is his property; it belongs to him more than the conquests of Semiramis belonged to that woman. One must hold onto the good action one has been capable of, and to a strong and bold thought that one has managed to produce. Modesty is the virtue of mediocrity. Why not render justice to oneself, and claim it for oneself as one would for others?"

We parted ways at Myus, a small Ionian town, halfway between Priene and Miletus. It is there that the Meander, after so many detours, finally falls into the sea, and regrets not having made even more in such an agreeable region.

Fatigued by the heat, I went to take refuge in an old, partially opened temple, because the <term>neokoros</term> <gloss>temple warden</gloss> was cleaning it at that moment. In the back of the sanctuary, I distinguished, not without difficulty because of the dim light, the seated statue of an old man covered in a long, very dirty cloak. His shoulder was burdened with a dusty axe.

<summary>The narrator discusses the legitimacy of claiming intellectual credit with Mandraites before parting ways in Myus. Seeking shelter from the heat in a temple, he encounters a mysterious, neglected statue.</summary>
<keywords>Thales, Mandraites, Myus, intellectual property, genius, temple, statue</keywords>

up the mountain without waiting for me at all,
and I was somewhat angered by this,
seeing myself left there mocked.
And so I watched behind them a while,
then [I went] to follow them, without having other arms
than I now have, until night had come
and took them from my sight.

**81.**
Now you know the reason for my absence,
oh dear father, and be certain of this.“
The father, whose name was Girafone,
it seemed to him he understood that veiled speech,
and he knew well and held the opinion,
as one wise and experienced in such things,
that they must have been nymphs
whom he said were such beautiful does.

**82.**
But in order not to make him a liar in this,
and so it would not seem that he noticed it,
and in order not to increase his desire
<margin>[greater</margin>
to follow them further, and also, if he could,
to cause him to put away this love himself
and, without revealing it to him, to cast it down,
he made a show of believing what he had said,
then he began to speak in such a manner:

<summary>Africo continues his lie to his father, Girafone, describing his failed attempt to capture the does. Girafone, being wise, realizes his son is actually pursuing nymphs, but decides to pretend he believes the story to prevent further obsession.</summary>

<note>A woodblock illustration depicts a mountainous landscape with a figure walking along a path near a waterfall and trees.</note>

Boarding a boat and waiting for a favorable wind,
The moon’s light is dim and hazy.
You wish to depart on a fragrant wheel,
But high mountains stretch for thousands of layers.

▲ Like moonlight hidden behind clouds, your heart will be clouded and prone to confusion.
▲ Those who receive this oracle should not act with haste.
▲ In all matters, you must wait for the right time.
▲ Pray to the gods and Buddhas to find peace of mind.
▲ The mention of high mountains stretching for thousands of layers represents the presence of many obstacles.

Charles, however, having been called and requested, began his journey toward Italy in order to restore the Roman Church, which had been disturbed by factions, to its former security. With Italy and the other borders pacified, he finally set out for Rome.

There, after several days, an inquiry was made into the crimes that had been alleged against Pope Leo <note>Pope Leo III</note> by his adversaries. Since no one could prove them, the Pope himself, before all the people in the Basilica of St. Peter, carrying the Gospel, ascended the pulpit. Having invoked the name of the Most Holy Trinity, he cleared himself of those charges by oath. *Baronius, Year of Christ 800.*

The seditious Roman citizens, some of whom were princes of the city and who had treated the Pope very poorly, were ordered by Charles to be beheaded in the Lateran Field <note>original: "Campo Lateranensi"</note>, three hundred in number. The clergy, however, were exiled to Gaul. *Calvisius, <note>Seth Calvisius, German chronologist</note> Year of Christ 800.*

And furthermore, he was saluted as Emperor Augustus by Leo and by all the Roman people, at which time he had already reigned in Francia for thirty-three years.

Charles, however, having been called and invited, began his journey toward Italy so that he might restore the Roman Church, which had been disturbed by factions, to its former security. Italy and the other regions having been pacified, he finally set out for Rome.

There, after several days, an inquiry having been made regarding the crimes that had been leveled against Pope Leo by his adversaries; since no one could prove them, the Pope himself, before all the people in the Basilica of St. Peter, carrying the Gospel, ascended the pulpit, and having invoked the name of the Most Holy Trinity, cleared himself of them by oath. *Baronius, Year of Christ 800.*

Three hundred seditious Roman citizens, some of whom were Princes of the City, who had treated the Pope very badly, were ordered by Charles to be beheaded in one day on the Lateran Field. The clergy, however, were relegated into exile in Gaul. *Calvisius, <note>Seth Calvisius, a 16th-century chronologist</note> Year of Christ 800.*

And furthermore, he was saluted as Emperor Augustus by Leo and by all the Roman people, when he had already reigned in France for thirty-three years.

In the time of the emperor Theophilus, Scholasticius the door-keeper was chamberlain, and in the time of Michael, son of Theophilus, the patrician Damian was chamberlain and after him, in the same reign, Basil, the Christ-loving emperor, was chamberlain. In the time of Basil, the Christ-loving sovereign, there was no chamberlain during all his reign. In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Samonas was chamberlain, and after him, in the time of the same emperor, the patrician Constantine. In the time of Alexander the emperor, the patrician Barbatus was chamberlain; and in the time of Constantine, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Constantine, mentioned before in the time of the sovereign Leo, was chamberlain again; and in the time of the sovereign Romanus, the patrician Theophanes; and in the second reign of Constantine, the patrician Basil.

In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving and ever-memorable emperor, lived the late Ktenas, an aged cleric of great wealth, who was precentor of the New Church and was skilled in singing as was no other at that time. This same Ktenas besought the patrician Samonas, who was at that time chamberlain, to intercede for him with the emperor so that he might be made <term>protospatharius</term> <gloss>a high court rank, literally "first sword-bearer"</gloss> and wear the shirt <note>referring to a ceremonial garment of office</note> and go in procession to the Lausiacus <note>a ceremonial hall in the Great Palace of Constantinople</note> and take his seat as <term>protospatharius</term> and receive a stipend of one pound, and in respect of this remuneration might give the emperor forty pounds. But the emperor could not bring himself to do this, saying that it was out of his power, and "to the great disgrace of my imperial majesty if a cleric becomes <term>protospatharius</term>." On hearing this from the patrician Samonas, this same Ktenas added to the forty pounds a pair of ear-rings valued at ten pounds, and a silver table with animals on it in gold relief, also valued at ten pounds. And the emperor, besought by the request of the patrician Samonas, the chamberlain, took the forty pounds of gold and the pair of ear-rings and the table with its gold on silver relief work, so that the total gift of the same Ktenas amounted to sixty pounds. Then the emperor made him <term>protospatharius</term>, and he received a stipend on that occasion of one pound. After being honoured with the rank of <term>protospatharius</term> this same Ktenas lived two years and then died; and he received a stipend of one pound for each of the two years.

<summary>The text documents the list of imperial chamberlains from the reign of Theophilus to Constantine VII and recounts the bribery of Emperor Leo VI by the cleric Ktenas to secure a court title.</summary>
<keywords>chamberlain, court rank, Ktenas, Samonas, imperial administration, protospatharius, Leo VI</keywords>

O eternal King, by what miserable fate is every man closed? # Absolution.

It is prohibited to confess sins sacramentally to an absent confessor via letters or a messenger, and to obtain absolution from the same absent party, under penalty of excommunication incurred automatically and reserved to the Roman Pontiff. No one is to defend, teach, print, or in any way put into practice such a proposition, even as one that might be considered probable in any case. Conversely, absolution from censures can indeed be conferred upon one who is absent, whether by letter, by messenger, or by another act that expresses the intention of the one absolving, as is evident from the rescripts and Bulls of Pontiffs directed to certain persons. The reason is that excommunication is an ecclesiastical penalty that can be inflicted even upon the absent, and therefore it can also be remitted.

13. The question arises: To whom should absolution be denied, and to whom should it be deferred?

Response: Judgment on this is left to the prudence of the confessor according to the circumstances that arise. However, it must be denied or deferred to those who are indisposed and who approach without having first examined their conscience; to those who lack the intention not to sin in the future; to those lacking supernatural contrition or attrition for their sins; to those unwilling to obey the confessor when he prescribes remedies to prevent them from relapsing; to those who are ignorant of the mysteries that are necessary by necessity of means; to those who are negligent in learning things necessary by necessity of precept; to those who do not make restitution when they are able to do so; to those who exist in the proximate occasion of sin, according to the points to be discussed under the heading *Proximate Occasion*; likewise, in any case or to those bound by a reserved excommunication; and finally, when there is no hope of amendment. See the heading *Custom*. Let confessors therefore weigh these matters,

<translation page="24">
# PROLEGOMENA

it was necessary to follow. But he himself expresses the true occasion shortly in the preface, namely because he saw many things being written by many people that were not sufficiently verified; and therefore he wished to consult for the sake of posterity, so that the Church might have a verified and solid Evangelical history. And Eusebius recognizes this occasion in Book 3, Chapter 24, as do Epiphanius in Book 2 against heresies, and Nicephorus, etc.

<margin>Argument: Luke began the history of the Gospel more deeply than the others, etc.</margin>
He begins the Evangelical history more deeply than the other two, namely Matthew and Mark, did, who, with Luke, pursue the history of the humanity [of Christ] in the first place. For, not content to start the matter from the Baptism of John and the Genealogy of Christ, he also resumes those things that pertain to the conception of both Christ and John the Baptist: likewise the birth of each, and what happened in these times. From there, he finally progresses to the doctrine of Christ; likewise, what he did. He is diligent and copious in miracles; for he indicates the occasions, the fruits, and other circumstances. He adorns the life of Christ with human affections, and those prone to gratification, such that sin is absent; he provides companions for Christ everywhere, whether disciples who are extremely simple, or crowds eager to learn; he provides adversaries who are extremely persistent, the Jews, and from among these, the Pharisees, and the Pontiffs
</translation>

<translation page="25">
# IN LUKE.

Scribes, and Elders, with whom the care of religion ought to have rested. The other listeners, for the most part, bring minds ready to understand. Finally, having entered into the history of the Passion, he studiously indicates its true external causes, Christ everywhere being foreknowing and prepared for death; and what happened before death, in death, and after death. Finally, he concludes the history with the glorious return to the heavens, from whence we still expect him as Judge of the living and the dead.

<margin>Status.</margin>
The status is <term>pragmatike</term> <gloss>pragmatic/historical</gloss>, because the history of deeds is woven together, and many <term>deiktika</term> <gloss>demonstrative elements</gloss> are added here, for everywhere he shows by whom, where, what, and how each thing was done.

<margin>Genus.</margin>
The style of speech in Luke is flourishing, and clear in the historical manner. And as for the words, the form of the discourse seems humble; for it lowers itself to the popular custom of speaking purely, yet not like Matthew and Mark. The style of Luke is somewhat more polished, yet it does not rise to Demosthenic pomp and the pagan splendor of words; and therefore it is <term>euschemon</term> <gloss>decorous/proper</gloss>, the sort of attire that befits a history of truth. In treatment, it is <term>haple diegesis</term> <gloss>simple narrative</gloss>, a bare explanation of matters, in which there is <term>aletheia</term> <gloss>truth</gloss> and <term>sapheneia</term> <gloss>clarity</gloss>, the truth of history and the perspicuity of the argument.

But if you look at the thing itself, it is grave.
</translation>

<summary>This text discusses the occasion of Luke's Gospel, highlighting his detailed account of Christ's early life, and evaluates the stylistic and rhetorical qualities of his narrative as a clear, historical, and decorous account.</summary>
<keywords>Luke, Gospel, Eusebius, Epiphanius, Nicephorus, Christ, Passion, status, style, history</keywords>

Even if it were otherwise, I would be neither the first to have produced this, nor is it as ridiculous among philosophers as he thinks. But I shall not digress from my purpose for these matters. The contemplation of the Fabrian System calls me, namely the one by which he trusts the phenomena around Saturn can be conveniently explained after he has demolished mine. For those earlier parts, with which he undertakes to order the motion of Saturn itself with new laws, are irrelevant here, nor would it be worth the effort to examine them. I wonder, however, what displeased him about the Tychonic hypothesis, that he was led to construct a new one from its foundations; an hypothesis which I fear Astronomers can hardly grasp, let alone approve.

But the part that pertains to the phases of Saturn is in no way clearer, and furthermore it is so far removed from all reason and likelihood that I do not know if it needs to be refuted by me. For whom, I ask, will this ridiculous conceit deceive, concerning those four little globes nearest to Saturn, of which two shine with the light of the Sun, and the other two reflect no rays at all, but by their own nature are most obscure? I seem to myself to be watching a circular
pages.19: game of counters, where some are white and others are black, being shown and hidden by turns, now these, now those. For such is the nature of that marvelous hypothesis. And why indeed did you not at least express in your diagram the circles which this new brood of planets follows? Circles which we would see not having Saturn in the center, nor indeed one smaller circle enclosed by a larger, but rather pairs lying one after another behind the planet, in each of which two of those satellites would run in such a way that one would never catch up to the other, but would always remain at a diameter's distance. Unless I am mistaken, I have correctly understood the mind of Fabrius; if not, I wish to be corrected, for it was something that had to be guessed. Furthermore, since he says that with these things posited, the phases 1, 4, 8, and 9 of his table are easily explained, I would like to know how the new planets grow from the smallest to the largest. For in Figures 1 and 4, they do not even have half the diameter of the central body of Saturn, whereas in Figures 8 and 9, it is necessary that they be equal to it, or even larger. Then, how will the phase of Eustachius himself observed in Figure 10 be deduced from this hypothesis? Since neither can round bodies make elliptical arcs, and the black planets here must be smaller than the white ones, contrary to what was posited: for they are settled, after some deliberation, to be equal to one another. Furthermore, what is the period of these new planets? Not a small matter, for he says it has not yet been discovered. But I fear that it is impossible for any such period to exist. For in the space of three years, of which the first was 1646, Eustachius affirms in a certain table, dedicated to the Most Serene Grand Duke of Tuscany, brother of the Most Eminent Cardinal, that this single Figure 10 appeared to him; from which it follows that the satellites must have moved nothing in the meantime, which could indeed be noticed. Yet afterwards in three other years, namely 1655 and the two following, they progressed to such an extent that in the middle of these years Saturn was seen as round, but at both extremes as having two orbs at its sides,

So that we might avoid this fraud, certain following signs seem entirely worthy of observation. Just as the unicorn horn is believed by the common people to sweat in the presence of poison. Now, indeed, if one asks whether and by what reason it could come about that it emits a true sweat, the matter is quite stuck. Sweating is certainly an intrinsic effect excited by the benefit of the soul, and the unicorn horn, insofar as it is torn from the body and to be used for medical purposes, lacks that soul; whence, then, is the effect? Should we flee to occult qualities? But truly, neither do these act above their powers. Andreas Baccius, in the cited location, indeed reports on the horns of the Cerastes <note>a certain species of serpent; Albertus Magnus, Ulysses Aldrovandus, Lord Johannes Veslingius (as cited by Bartholinus, p. 6), Jonston, and others make mention of it</note>: likewise, a certain kind of stone, of a dark, murky color, which they call "serpentine tongue," also sweats in the presence of poison, but analogically or improperly; just as we see all polished and shiny objects, surrounded by the humidity of the air, when heat approaches, become altered in a certain way and, as it were, emit a sweat. But since that effect, or clouding, occurs from elsewhere even in the absence of poison, it is not something we should accept as an undoubted sign.

Conversely, you put a piece of bread into a very pure vessel filled with water and apply the unicorn horn in the same way as above, and you will see a wonderful effect, that while you remove the unicorn horn, the bread also follows little by little, in the way that Dr. Kergerus thinks, in *On Fermentation, Section 1, Chapter 5, page 46*, as iron follows the magnet by which it is drawn.

As for the truth of the matter, we shall not attempt to call it into doubt. > "Let the matter be made clearer by circular demonstration: If a coin floats, it depresses the water by its weight and is pushed by any body touching or intruding (not just the Unicorn horn), because the water adhering around it is higher than its horizon, which is depressed beneath the coin, with which the coin flows easily from a higher to a lower place; from a lower to a higher place, it ascends with difficulty. The coin rushes toward the coin because the water flows away around the lower part of each, seeks continuity, and finds rest not at the horizon of the vessel, but at least in equilibrium. A crumb of bread, on the other hand, around which the water is higher than the horizon, while it insinuates itself into the pores, rushes easily toward either the crumb or another body around which the water is higher, and wishes to rest in equilibrium. Finally, the coin rushes more easily to the sides of a dry vessel because the water adheres more deeply to the side there, but the crumb rushes to the sides of a wetted one because, being higher than the horizon on both sides, it joins itself more readily."

Therefore, there is no need to have recourse to occult qualities in a matter of such little moment.

that both are Universals. The reason for the former is this: because that which is subjectible, as such, is not predicable, as is self-evident; therefore, since a Logical Universal is predicable, the subjectible, as such, will not be a Logical universal. But since a metaphysical universal is situated neither in predicability nor in subjectibility, but in the inexistence of one thing in many, just as the subjectible, as such, can still be one thing apt to be in many, so too it will be able to be a metaphysical universal. The reason for the latter is because a Genus, which is subjectible (for example, animal with respect to living), is also predicable with respect to rational and irrational.

VII. Q. *Whether a Genus in general is predicated univocally of a Genus of real being and a Genus of a being of reason?* I answer. These two Genera, according to their material parts alone, agree with one another analogically; because Being can only be predicated analogically of real being and a being of reason. But if they are taken in the being of a genus, and as they are of Logical consideration; since the Logical artifice and concept of both are precisely the same, there is no doubt that they agree with one another univocally.

VIII. Q. *Since the highest Genus is as far removed from the lowest as the lowest Genus is from the Species; why is the lowest Genus a different universal than the species; and the highest Genus not different from the lowest genus?* I answer. That this diversity is not to be sought from the greater or lesser distance that universals have in the predicamental line; but from their quidditative concept. Since, therefore, both the highest Genus and the lowest Genus are predicated as a material part; while the species is predicated as the whole essence; there can be no doubt that the species differs more from the lowest Genus than the latter does from the highest.

IX. Q. *Whether the concept defining a designated Genus is the concept that formally makes an exercised Genus?* I answer. Since the concept making a Genus in the exercised act must also make a universal in the exercised act; and a universal cannot be made by a simple concept not abstracting from a multitude; and the concept defining a designated Genus does not abstract from a multitude; just as it is a simple concept, so it is not a concept making a Genus in the exercised act. Therefore, by the definition of a Genus, a Genus is defined as designated, but it is not made as exercised.

X. Q. *What is a species taken in general?* I answer. Although it is certain that a metaphysical species taken in general can rightly be called, *One thing apt to exist in many as the whole essence*; yet because there is a huge distinction between this and a Logical species, one might not undeservedly ask whether, since a Logical universal is predicable, a definition in general can be given for a Logical Species? Hence there is deep silence everywhere among authors regarding this definition, as they always define a species either only as predicable or only as subjectible. We therefore believe that for a Species taken in general, as it includes both the Predicable and the subjectible, no better definition can be given than this: (*One thing apt as the whole essence to terminate a proposition*). We do not wish to assert, however, that others have acted wrongly while they first divided the species, and first defined it once divided. For 
</translation>

<translation page="19">
<header>ON THE UNIVERSAL IN SPECIE.</header>

since a subjectible species, in the being of a Universal and of a Logical species, does not agree univocally with the Predicable; and those things which do not agree univocally with one another ought, according to Aristotle, to be divided first and defined afterwards, it is clear that authors dealing only with a Logical species, that is, as it is one of the predicables, rightly defined only the species already divided.

XI. Question. *By what reason should a Predicable and subjectible species be defined?* Answer. A Predicable species is *One thing apt as the whole essence to be predicated of many.* A subjectible species, however, is *That which is subjected to a genus, or which is the same thing, one thing apt to be the subject of a proposition as the whole essence.* For since the discussion here is only about a natural proposition; if the predicate is broader than the subject, which is the species, then by this very fact it must be a genus; therefore in the present case, to be the subject of a proposition is the same as to be subjected to a genus.

XII. Question. *Whether besides the said species, no other remains?* Answer. There is still another species, the subaltern, and another, the lowest, as the common opinion holds. The lowest is, *One thing apt as the whole essence to be predicated of many differing only in number.* For example, man, who is predicated of Francis, Peter, Paul, and others differing among themselves only in number. A subaltern, however, is: *One thing apt to be subjected as the whole essence; and to be predicated as a material part.* Because, clearly, it is itself, as Porphyry says in the second chapter, genus and species, but in a different respect.

XIII. Question. *Whether for a Genus to differ from a species, it suffices that the latter be predicated as the whole essence, the former as a material part: since living, for example, is a genus and a species, and includes the same constitutive elements, namely, an animated body?* Answer. Between a Genus and a species taken materially, the aforementioned distinction is sufficient, but not between a Genus and a species taken formally. For the concept making a species formally must be complex, conceiving *animated body* as genus and difference in such a way that, by the power of that concept, these two become *one thing apt to be predicated of many as the whole essence.* But if *animated body* is conceived by a simple concept, then it will be the same as *living*, which is a Genus and not a species taken formally. Furthermore, there is a difference between the concept making a subaltern and a lowest species, for the object of a concept making a subaltern species cannot be given so precisely from the side of the thing. For example, there is no object given that is precisely an *animated body*. However, the object of the concept making a lowest species is given from the side of the thing, for example, *a roaring animal*.

XIV. Question. *Since a part cannot be formally predicated of the whole; but a Genus is a part of the species, which is the whole; how can it be said that a Genus can be formally predicated of the species?* Answer. A part, indeed, cannot be formally predicated of the whole when taken in the abstract; but it can when taken in the concrete. Hence, although I cannot rightly say formally: *man is animality*, I do rightly say: *man is an animal*.

XV. Question. *Since the lowest species is only predicable of individuals, it cannot be understood unless it is certain what an Individual is; what therefore is understood by the name of Individual?* Answer.

### Castor Oil <note>original: "Oleum Cicinum"</note>

In Gelisco, a province of New Spain, a certain oil or liquid is brought in, to which the Spaniards have given the name "oil of the infernal fig," because it is extracted from a tree that is similar to the <term>Ricinus</term> <gloss>castor-oil plant</gloss> in both its fruit and its leaves, but which grows to a greater height due to the richness of the soil.

<margin>Oil of the infernal fig.</margin>

Indeed, the Indians extract this oil by the same method that Dioscorides taught in Book 1, Chapter 30: that is, by bruising the seed, then boiling it in water, and finally skimming off the oil that floats on top with spoons. This method of extracting oils from seeds and fruits is very familiar to the Indians, who know nothing of expression <note>i.e., pressing</note>; but this oil is also extracted more easily in this way than by expression.

<margin>Method of extracting oils.</margin>

<translation page="9">### XXVIII.

And anyone may lend his money, whether in his own name <note>Digest, book 12, title 1, law 2, paragraph "penultimate"</note> or in another's, and whether in the name of one who knows <note>Digest, book 12, title 1, law 2, paragraph "penultimate"; law 9, paragraph 8; law 15</note> or one who is ignorant of it. <note>Digest, book 12, title 1, law 9, last paragraph</note> However, no one can give another's money as a loan for consumption against the owner's will or without his knowledge, since he does not transfer it to the recipient. <note>Digest, book 12, title 1, law 2, paragraph "penultimate"; law 11, last paragraph; law 13, in the beginning and paragraph 1; law 56, paragraph 2; Digest on suretyship, law 20, in the beginning; Digest on the acquisition of the ownership of things, law 54; Digest on the Rules of Law, law 54</note>

### XXIX.

Those prohibited from giving a loan for consumption are: I. The insane. <note>Digest, book 12, title 1, law 12; Digest on Obligations and Actions, law 24; Code on contracting sales, law 2; Digest on the Rules of Law, law 5</note> II. Wards <term>pupilli</term> <gloss>children under guardianship</gloss> without the authorization of their tutors. <note>Digest, book 12, title 1, law 19, paragraph 1; Digest on the Macedonian Decree of the Senate, law 3, paragraph 2; Digest on the authority of tutors, law 9, in the beginning; Institutes, book 1, title 21, paragraph 2</note> III. Spendthrifts <term>prodigi</term> <gloss>those who squander their wealth</gloss> who have been interdicted from their property. <note>Digest on the obligations of words, law 6; Digest on the curator of the insane, law 10</note>

### XXX.

Children under parental power <term>filiifamilias</term> <gloss>persons still under the power of their father</gloss>, as well as slaves, to whom the free administration of their <term>peculium</term> <gloss>private fund or savings</gloss> has been granted, can give a loan for consumption from their master's money, as found in the law on pacts, <note>Digest, book 2, title 14, law 28</note> or from their <term>peculium</term> coins, as found in the Digest on this title, <note>Digest, book 12, title 1, law 2, paragraph "penultimate"</note> (for in truth the ownership of the items in the <term>peculium</term> belongs to the master or the father, <note>Code on paternal power, law 2; Institutes, book 2, title 9, paragraphs 1 and 2</note> even if the children or slaves are meanwhile imagined to be the owners, <note>Digest on the peculium, law 17</note> and their own patrimony is said to be their own <note>Digest on the peculium, law 5, paragraph 3; law 32, in the end of the beginning; law 52, in the end of the beginning; law 47, paragraph "final"; Institutes, book 4, title 7, paragraph 10</note>), so that the obligation or action is acquired for the master or father. <note>Digest, book 12, title 1, law 2, paragraph "penultimate", joined with law 11, last paragraph</note>

### XXXI.

But what of a person who has reached puberty but is under 25 years of age? Can he give a loan for consumption without the consent of his curator? Although the negative opinion relies on the authority of many learned doctors, I, with the most distinguished and learned Lord Doctor Meier, my teacher whom I greatly revere <note>in the disputation on the loan for consumption, thesis 24, and in the "Illustrious Questions" on book 2 of the Institutes of Justinian, question 40</note>, shall maintain the affirmative.

### XXXII.

A partner of all goods likewise cannot lend money that he acquired after the partnership was contracted—even though it is not common property by law itself, but the property of the one acquiring it, and owed to the partners only in part—without the consent of the other</translation>

<translation page="10">partners, in such a way that the whole becomes a loan for consumption. <note>Digest, book 12, title 1, law 16; Digest on the partnership, law 74; Code on common legacies, law 3, paragraph 2</note>

### XXXIII.

Governors of provinces, and those who are around them, that is, the officials they bring with them into the province, are prohibited for the duration of their office, by special reason, from giving a loan for consumption in that province, either by themselves or through others. <note>Digest, book 12, title 1, law 33; Code if a certain thing is sought, law 3</note>

### XXXIV.

However, this prohibition does not include the officials who serve the magistrates, <note>Digest, book 12, title 1, law 34</note> nor urban magistrates in the city, <note>Code on the contracts of judges, law 1</note> nor perpetual magistrates, nor those who hold a magistracy in their own homeland, because naturally the reason for the prohibition ceases.

### XXXV.

Fathers of families <term>patresfamilias</term> <gloss>heads of households</gloss> who are of their own right can regularly receive a loan for consumption. <note>The entire title of the Digest and Code on the Macedonian Decree of the Senate; Digest, book 1, title 6, law 4</note>

### XXXVI.

However, the ward <term>pupillus</term> <gloss>child under guardianship</gloss> is prohibited from receiving a loan without the authority of his tutor, <note>Digest, book 12, title 1, law 19, paragraph 1; Digest on Obligations and Actions, law 59</note> as are the insane and the spendthrift <term>prodigus</term> <gloss>one who squanders wealth</gloss> who has been interdicted from his property. <note>Argument from Digest, book 12, title 1, law 32, joined with Digest on the Rules of Law, laws 5 and 40; Digest on the obligations of words, law 6; Digest on the curator of the insane, law 10; Digest on minors, law 27, in the beginning</note>

### XXXVII.

But here a doubt arises: who is called a spendthrift? Is it the one to whom interdiction is applied by law alone, as Donellus intended <note>Book 12 of the Commentaries on Civil Law, chapter 22</note> and Fachinaeus <note>Controversies, 2, 63</note>, or is it the one to whom administration is forbidden by the decree of a magistrate? Since the latter opinion is more widely accepted and more consistent with the texts and the reason of the law, it appeals to me as well.

### XXXVIII.

Anyone also, for a singular reason, ineffectually gives money as a loan to a profligate youth, whom he knows will squander the money. <note>Digest on mandate, law 12, paragraph 11; Digest on minors, law 24, paragraph 4</note> It is also ineffectually given to a son under parental power; but as to its effect, insofar as the creditor is repelled by the exception of the Macedonian Decree of the Senate. <note>Digest on the action for indebitum, law 40, in the beginning; the entire title of the Digest on the Macedonian Decree of the Senate</note></translation>

<summary>These pages address the legal requirements and prohibitions regarding who may enter into loan contracts, specifically covering the agency of slaves, the status of minors and spendthrifts, and the restrictions placed on provincial officials.</summary>
<keywords>Mutuum, Loan for Consumption, Legal Capacity, Peculium, Macedonian Decree of the Senate, Spendthrifts, Wards</keywords>

### XXIX.

Those prohibited from giving a loan for consumption are: I. The insane <note>original: "l. 12. ff. h. t. l. 24. ff. de O. & A. l. 2. C. de contrah. empt. l. 5. ff. de R. I." Pupils <term>pupilli</term> <gloss>wards under puberty</gloss> without the authorization of their tutors <note>original: "l. 19. §. 1. ff. h. t. l. 3. §. 2. ff. de SC. (law 6, Digest on verbal obligations; law 10, Digest on the curator of the insane)</note>.

### XXX.

Children under parental power, just as slaves, to whom the free administration of a peculium <term>peculium</term> <gloss>a sum of money or property managed by a subordinate</gloss> has been granted, can give as a loan for consumption the master's money, as is in <note>original: "l. 28. de pact." (law 28, on pacts)</note>, or peculiary coins, as is in <note>original: "l. 2. §. pen. ff. h. t." (law 2, § penultimate, Digest on this title)</note> (for in truth the ownership of peculiary things belongs to the master or father <note>original: "l. 2. C. de patr. potest. §. 1. 2. Inst. per quas pers. cuiq. acquir." (law 2, Code on parental power; § 1 & 2, Institutes on through which persons property is acquired)</note>, although children under parental power or slaves are meanwhile imagined to be the owners <note>original: "l. 17. ff. de pecul." (law 17, Digest on the peculium)</note>, and it is said to be their own patrimony <note>original: "l. 5. §. 3. l. 32. in fin. pr. l. 52. in fin. pr. l. 47. §. fin. ff. de pecul. §. 10. Inst. de Act." (law 5, § 3; law 32, in the end of the beginning; law 52, in the end of the beginning; law 47, § final, Digest on the peculium; § 10, Institutes on Actions)</note>), so that the obligation or action is acquired for the master or father <note>original: "l. 2. §. pen. juncta l. 11. §. ult. ff. h. t." (law 2, § penultimate, joined with law 11, § last, Digest on this title)</note>.

### XXXI.

But what of a person past puberty but under 25 years of age; can he give a loan for consumption without the consent of his curator? And although the negative opinion rests upon the authorities of many doctors, I, however, with the most distinguished and learned Doctor Meier, my most highly esteemed teacher <note>original: "in disp. de Mutuo thes. 24. & in quaestionibus illustribus ad lib. 2. Institutionum Justinianearum quaest. 40." (in the dissertation on loan for consumption, thesis 24, and in the illustrious questions on book 2 of the Justinian Institutes, question 40)</note>, shall maintain the affirmative.

### XXXII.

A partner of all goods also cannot lend money that he acquired after the partnership was contracted—although by the law itself it is not common property, but the property of the acquirer, and due to the partners only in part—without the consent of the other
pages.10:
partners, in such a way that the whole becomes a loan for consumption <note>original: "lex 16. Digesta hoc titulo lex 74. Digesta pro socio. et lex 3. paragrapho 2. Codex communis de legatis." (law 16, Digest on this title; law 74, Digest on partnership; and law 3, paragraph 2, Code common on legacies)</note>.

### XXXIII.

Presidents of provinces, as well as those who are around them, that is, the ministers whom they bring with them into the province, are, during their office, prohibited for a special reason from giving money as a loan for consumption in that province, either by themselves or through others <note>original: "lex 33. Digesta hoc titulo lex 3. Codex si certum petetur." (law 33, Digest on this title; law 3, Code if a certain thing is sought)</note>.

### XXXIV.

However, officials who serve the magistrates are not included in this prohibition <note>original: "lex 34. Digesta hoc titulo" (law 34, Digest on this title)</note>, nor are urban magistrates in the city <note>original: "lex unica Codex de contractibus judicum." (the only law, Code on the contracts of judges)</note>, just as neither are perpetual magistrates, or those who hold office in their own homeland: because, indeed, the reason for the prohibition ceases.

### XXXV.

Fathers of families who are of their own right can regularly receive a loan for consumption <note>original: "toto titulo Digesta et Codex de Senatusconsulto Macedoniano." (the entire title, Digest and Code on the Macedonian Senate-Consult; "lex 4. Digesta de his qui sui vel alieni juris sunt." (law 4, Digest on those who are of their own or another's right)</note>.

### XXXVI.

Pupils are prohibited from receiving a loan for consumption without the authorization of a tutor <note>original: "lex 19. paragrapho 1. Digesta hoc titulo lex 59. Digesta de Obligationibus et Actionibus" (law 19, paragraph 1, Digest on this title; law 59, Digest on Obligations and Actions)</note>, as are the insane and the prodigal to whom his property has been interdicted <note>original: "argumento lex 32. Digesta hoc titulo juncta lex 5. et 40. Digesta de Regulis Juris lex 6. Digesta de Verborum Obligationibus lex 10. Digesta de curatore furiosi lex 27. principio Digesta de minoribus." (by argument of law 32, Digest on this title, joined with law 5 and 40, Digest on Rules of Law; law 6, Digest on Verbal Obligations; law 10, Digest on the curator of the insane; law 27, in the beginning, Digest on minors)</note>.

### XXXVII.

But here a doubt occurs: who is called a prodigal? Is it he for whom interdiction occurs by law alone? Donellus indeed wished so <note>original: "liber 12. commentariorum juris civilis caput 22." (book 12 of the commentaries on civil law, chapter 22)</note>, and Fachinaeus <note>original: "2. controversiarum 63." (2, controversies 63)</note>. Or is it he for whom administration is interdicted by the decree of a magistrate? Since this latter opinion is more accepted, and more agreeable to the texts and the reason of the law, it pleases me as well.

### XXXVIII.

Also, for a singular reason, anyone uselessly gives money as a loan for consumption to a profligate adolescent whom they know will squander the money <note>original: "lex 12. paragrapho 11. Digesta mandati lex 24. paragrapho 4. Digesta de minoribus." (law 12, paragraph 11, Digest on mandate; law 24, paragraph 4, Digest on minors)</note>. Uselessly also to a child under parental power; but by reason of its effect, insofar as the creditor is repelled by the exception of the Macedonian Senate-Consult <note>original: "lex 40. in principio Digesta de condictione indebiti toto titulo Digesta de Senatusconsulto Macedoniano." (law 40, in the beginning, Digest on the recovery of what was not due; the entire title, Digest on the Macedonian Senate-Consult)</note>.

XXXIII. Regarding imaginary time, we judge the same as we do regarding imaginary space: namely, that outside of the intrinsic durations of things, which found various relations of distance and proximity, it is in reality nothing at all.

XXXIV. Finally, duration is either created or uncreated. The uncreated is proper to GOD alone and is called Eternity. It is defined by <term>Boethius</term> <gloss>Roman philosopher, c. 480–524</gloss>: *The simultaneous and perfect possession of interminable life.* Created duration is either temporary or perpetual. Temporary is that which has both a beginning and an end. Perpetual is that which, at least, does not have an end. Such is the duration of the Angels and the rational soul, which is also called an <term>aevum</term> <gloss>age/duration of spirits</gloss>, and is commonly defined as: *The interminable permanence of a thing in a state once received.*

### ON QUANTITY.

XXXV. Aristotle describes a <term>quantum</term> <gloss>quantity</gloss> here in Book 5, text 18: *That which is divisible into things that are present within it, of which each one is a certain "one," and this "something" is apt to be.* That is (as Father <term>Suarez</term> <gloss>Francisco Suárez, 1548–1617, Spanish Jesuit philosopher</gloss> interprets), those things which are each apt by their own nature to remain as a certain whole, separated from others, and which is divisible according to the force of quantity—namely, through physical and natural divisibility—by the force of which one body naturally expels another, or its parts, from the place they previously occupied.

XXXVI. There is an opinion, as Father <term>Suarez</term> says, sufficiently common among the Thomists, that the primary formal effect of quantity is the distinction of integral parts, such that without quantity neither prime matter nor any other material entity has any integral parts. Therefore, the primary formal effect of quantity cannot consist in the distinction of parts.

<translation page="20">These are the words of Strabo: "In Crete, the sacred rites of Jove are performed in a particular manner, with orgiastic rituals. They called 'Curetes' certain youths who danced in armor." They also add a story regarding the NATAL ORIGINS OF JOVE, saying that Saturn was accustomed to swallowing his children as soon as they were born. Rhea, however, tried to hide her labor pains and steal away the infant once born, and to save him as much as possible. To this end, with the help of the Curetes, who armed themselves and danced with a tumult around the Goddess, playing drums and other instruments that produced a loud noise, they frightened Saturn and deceived him while they took his son away from him; and by the same effort, they nourished Jove, who had been entrusted to them. Some think they were called Curetes as if they were 'curators' <note>Latin: *curatores*</note>, either because they performed Jove's <term>kourotrophian</term> <gloss>rearing of a child</gloss> (that is, his nourishment), or because they served him. Suidas explains this when he asserts that the Curetes were Jove's nurses and guardians.

Arnobius, in his work *Against the Gentiles*, book 3, commemorates those Curetes who are said to have hidden Jove's crying at one time with cymbals, or in the manner of the Samothracian fingers, which the Greeks indicate are five in number and call the Idaean Dactyls. And elsewhere: "Was Jove saved from destruction by the benefit of the Curetes?" Whom they then led away to the hidden places of Mount Ida. Hence, Crete is called the island of great Jove. Relevant to our matter is the commentary of Servius, on book 4 of the *Georgics*, page 149: "Ops, the wife of Saturn, gave Jove to the Curetes, the Corybantes, and the Idaean Dactyls to be guarded on Mount Dictae of Crete, so that Saturn would not consume him, as he was accustomed to do with all his children."

> The Dictaean Curetes, they report, who long ago
> Are said to have hidden that crying of Jove in Crete,
> When boys, armed, beat bronze upon bronze in rhythm
> Around the boy with a nimble dance,
> Lest Saturn, having found him, consign him to his jaws
> And inflict an eternal wound upon the mother under his breast.

Thus wrote Lucretius, book 2. I will not pass over a very rare coin, dedicated to Antoninus Caracalla, celebrating DICTAEAN JOVE, minted by the Prasians, the people of Crete, regarding whom see Strabo, book 7, chapter 17, and the learned notes of Thomas de Pinedo on Stephanus, under "Prasus." The Deity sits holding a thunderbolt, around whom is read ZEYS DIKTAIOS <gloss>Jove Dictaean</gloss>, and below, PRASON <gloss>of the Prasians</gloss>. Moreover, the Cabiri were considered most powerful everywhere. They are called <term>apotropaioi theoi</term> <gloss>averting gods</gloss>, <term>alexikakoi</term> <gloss>warding off evils</gloss>, <term>lysioi</term> <gloss>releasing</gloss>, <term>phyxioi</term> <gloss>putting to flight</gloss>, according to Julius Pollux: Emissary Gods, repellers of evils, averting, releasing, and putting evils to flight. Varro, in *On the Latin Language*, book 4, calls them Great Gods, Chrestic Gods, Powerful Gods, and alongside him, Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book 3, [calls them] Great Gods, Good Gods, Powerful Gods. Apollodorus, in book 6 *On the Gods*, and Pausanias, in his *Boeotica*, write at length about them.

Some, however, have published works on Cretan and Phrygian matters, involving them in certain sacrifices, partly mystical and partly satisfied by some agreement, such as</translation>

<translation page="21">THE INFANCY OF JOVE, raised in Crete, and the ceremonies of the Mother of the Gods to be celebrated in Phrygia and on Trojan Ida. There is certainly great variety in these accounts, as some show them to be the same as the Curetes, the Corybantes, the Cabiri, the Idaean Dactyls, and the Telchines. In this, however, all agree that they are certain inspired spirits, and Bacchic, and in the tumultuous movement of arms, and with spirit and crash, and cymbals and drums, and arms as well, and pipes and shouting, they stun during the act of sacrificing. Thus Strabo, book 10. Of whom let us again hear Germanicus Caesar in his [commentary on] Aratus:

> Duty made the labor worthy,
> Because the companions of faith poured forth the first cradles of great
> Jove, thunderstruck, when the Corybantes, servants of the Lady,
> Beating brazen cymbals with deceptive right hand,
> Exercised the theft of the parent, lest the boy's crying
> Touch the ancestral airs.

Those initiated into the mysteries of the Curetes were believed to have the Gods most present in times of danger, and especially to be about to escape every tempest of the sea; furthermore, to become holier and more just. Therefore, many Heroes were imbued with their rites: Jason, Castor, Pollux, Hercules, Orpheus, according to Diodorus, book 5, page 223. The Scholiast of Apollonius, *Argonautica* book 1, verse 915, teaches that Ulysses and Agamemnon were initiated in the same way. Tarquinius, the son of Demaratus of Corinth, was mystically included in the Samothracian religions, says Macrobius, *Saturnalia* book 3, chapter 4. Plutarch, in [his life of] *Alexander*, reports that even Philip, the father of Alexander the Great, was initiated.

The coin seems to represent the bronze belts of the Cabiri and their painted tunics, bordered and fastened with brooches, called <term>trabeas</term> <gloss>robes of state</gloss>, with which Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 2, asserts they were adorned. "Then," says the same author, "they are each girded with a sword, holding a lance or rod in the right hand, and in the left a shield similar to a Thracian target." That shield is oblong and narrower, such as are said to be among the Greeks the armaments of those who have been initiated into the rites of the Curetes: All of which cannot more accurately express the habit of the three soldiers depicted on the coin. The same author, book 7, also commemorates bronze helmets distinguished by feathered crests. I believe those three soldiers were described by Strabo, book 10, as born from Vulcan and Cabira, daughter of Proteus, to whom three altars were built in the Roman Circus, namely to the Great and Powerful Gods, according to Tertullian, *On Spectacles*, chapter 8. But perhaps these things have been said about the Curetes more idly than was fitting: let us proceed to the remainder.

They seem not to contain themselves but to move impetuously, whence the ancients used <term>orcheisthai</term> <gloss>to dance</gloss> in place of <term>kineisthai kai erethizesthai</term> <gloss>to be moved and irritated</gloss>, according to Athenaeus, book 1 of the *Deipnosophistae*. <margin>
(u) folio 82, column 1.
(x) folio 25, Column I.
(*) see Ignatius in the Epistle to the Philadelphians and the 68th Apostolic Canon; also the author of the Apostolic Constitutions, Book 5, chapter 14.
(y) on fasting, chapter 14.
(z) Observations on Tertullian, Book 1, on Prayer, page 43 and following.
(a) Notes on Epiphanius, page 358.
(b) Book 7 of the Stromata.
(c) on fasting, Book 4, chapter 5, page 708.
(d) <term>Avoda Sara</term> <gloss>Idolatry</gloss>, folio 29, column 1.
(e) in Plutarch, in the Table Talk.
(f) see Tertullian, on fasting, chapter 1, page 701.
</margin>
That certain of the Jews fasted twice in every week, namely on the second and fifth days, is evident not only from the example of that Pharisee mentioned by Luke, but it is also clearly indicated in the Babylonian Talmud, in the tractate <term>Bava Kama</term> <gloss>First Gate</gloss> (u). The Hebrew masters in the Jerusalem Talmud, in the tractate <term>Megilla</term> <gloss>Scroll</gloss> (x), assign as the cause for this that Moses ascended the mountain to receive the tables of the Law on the fifth day of the week, and descended on the second day. If anyone compares this with the most celebrated fasts of the fourth and sixth days (*) customarily observed weekly in the Roman Church, they will discover no obscure signs of Pharisaism. For this reason, these fasts were never customary in the purer Church. For although they object to us the authority of Tertullian (y), it has long since been refuted by Rigaltius (z) that "stations" there do not refer to fasts, but to those assemblies instituted for the sake of prayer, with Petavius himself (a) in agreement. Indeed, what they oppose from Epiphanius and Clement of Alexandria (b) has been learnedly discussed by Daillé (c). It remains, therefore, for us to inquire whether that too went by the name of a fast among the Hebrews, when each person refrained from eating meat. I am not far from asserting this, since in the tractate <term>Avoda Sara</term> <gloss>Idolatry</gloss> (d) mention is made of <term>mamoni le-ta'anita</term> <gloss>a sum [of money] for a fast</gloss> intended for fish. Indeed, at that time, this perverse opinion had already settled into the minds of many, as if pleasures could not be restrained and lust subdued in any way other than by avoiding meat. <translation page="12">
### And as for the greeting of peace between a man and his fellow, and students of the wise,
### they do not greet anyone, but go about like those who are rebuked and excommunicated
### by God; and if an unlearned person offers them a greeting, they return it
### to him in a soft voice and with a heavy countenance.

*Salutations (on a day of fasting) are not very frequent between a man and his friend. Students of the wise, however, greet absolutely no one, but walk as if they are worthy of rebuke and separated from GOD. If, therefore, any of the common people greets them, they do indeed return the greeting, but with a subdued voice and a grave countenance. It is not permitted, however, to dwell on these things any longer, as the breadth of the subject leads us elsewhere.*

### §, III.

If anything else is involved, the Jubilees certainly grace this place; which every fiftieth year restored liberty to slaves, and returned lost or sold possessions to their masters. They observed this law, divinely prescribed, with the utmost religion until the desolation of the first Sanctuary. But after a long time had completed that fateful cycle of years, and the Jews had returned to their own lands, that [law] was never recalled, nor were the solemnities of the Jubilees celebrated.

(i) v. Maim. <term>Hilchot Shmita ve-Yovel</term> <gloss>Laws of Sabbatical and Jubilee Years</gloss>, Chapter X. Add Hottinger in <term>Analect. Historico-Theolog.</term> <gloss>Historical-Theological Analects</gloss>, Dissert III, p. 160.

The opinion of those who assert that the jubilees were instituted not in the forty-ninth, but exactly in the fiftieth year, is very favorable to this. For the Jews themselves properly distinguish between the <term>Yovel</term> <gloss>Jubilee</gloss> (or jubilee year) and the <term>Shmita</term> <gloss>Sabbatical year</gloss> (or year of remission).

If, therefore, someone from the common people greets them, they do indeed return the greeting, but with a low voice and a grave countenance. We are not permitted to dwell longer on these things, as the breadth of the subject leads us elsewhere.

### §. III.

If anything else is relevant, the Jubilees certainly grace this place, which restored liberty to slaves in every fiftieth year, and to their masters, possession of their lost and sold properties. This law, divinely prescribed, they observed with the highest religion until the desolation of the first Sanctuary. But after a long time had completed that fatal cycle of years, and the Jews had returned to their own lands, that law was never revoked, nor were the solemnities of the Jubilees celebrated.

That certain Jews fasted twice in each week, namely on the second and fifth days, is evident not only from the example of that Pharisee mentioned by Luke, but it is also clearly indicated in the Babylonian Talmud, in the tractate <term>Bava Kama</term> <gloss>First Gate</gloss> (u). The Hebrew masters in the Jerusalem Talmud, in the tractate <term>Megilla</term> <gloss>Scroll</gloss> (x), provide the reason for this: that Moses ascended the mountain to receive the tables of the Law on the fifth day of the week, and descended on the second day. If anyone compares this with the most celebrated fasts of the fourth and sixth days (*) that are customarily observed every week in the Roman Church, he will discover clear marks of Pharisaism. Therefore, these fasts were never in use in the purer Church. For although they object to us the authority of Tertullian (y), it has long since been refuted by Rigaltius (z) that by "stations" there, fasts are not understood, but rather those assemblies instituted for the sake of prayer, a view in which Petavius (a) himself concurs. Furthermore, the matter which they oppose using Epiphanius and Clement of Alexandria (b) has been learnedly discussed by Daillé (c). It remains, therefore, that we investigate whether it also came to be called a fast among the Hebrews when someone abstained from eating meat. I am not far from asserting this, since in the tractate <term>Avoda Sara</term> (d) mention is made of <term>memuni le-ta'anita</term> <gloss>fast-fish</gloss>. For at that time, a perverse opinion had already taken root in the minds of many, as if pleasures could not be curbed and lust restrained in any other way than by avoiding meat. This is entirely different from what Pythagoras (e) taught, who, in his symbol "do not taste fish" <note>original: "ἰχθύων μὴ γεύεσθαι"</note>, judged that the eating of fish pertains to luxury and superfluous delights. This error was propagated not only among the Montanists and Tatianists (f), but the Romanists also received it from the Jews by a kind of hereditary right. Finally, one must not omit what Gabriel Albaspinæus (g) reports: that it was once the custom that no one should be greeted with a kiss during a time of fasting, which the <term>Ordo Romanus</term> <gloss>Roman Order</gloss> and other writers on rites also confirm. For very similar and most closely related to this is the Hebrew custom which Maimonides (h) explains: <term>u-me'atin bi-she'ilat</term>

(h) <term>Hilchot Ta'anit</term> <gloss>Laws of Fasting</gloss>, chapter III, number 8. See the addition which Rabbi Joseph Karo cites from the Mishna and Gemara at this place.

<translation page="14">The purple-clad Mistress of deceits, consort of the royal bed, enters the arena. The supreme Commander of wars, Porphyrius, enters, surrounded by two cohorts of soldiers. Maximinus, the August Emperor of the East, enters; with eloquence and majesty, he offers the young Virgin honeyed enticements of pleasure, flatteries, and allurements, more powerful for persuasion than all torments. What does CATHARINE do in the face of these things? In a brief but sharp speech, she strips the Empress, the wife of Maximinus, and Porphyrius, the invincible Commander of the royal army, of the weapons of Impiety, clothes them in the breastplate of justice and the helmet of salvation, and captures them for the obedience of faith. Virgil, that phoenix of wits, tells how the olive tree of Hercules, dried up by the unfairness of time, barren of foliage, endowed with no greenness, when joined to a Laurel, sprouted again with severed trunks, spread into branches, curled into leaves, and offered a deep shade to travelers. So much did it profit to be joined to the Laurel. Let us extract the kernel of truth from the husk of the fables. The Empress, wife of Maximinus, who had withered in the barren arena of paganism, joined to the crowned Laurel CATHARINE, puts on the greenness of the orthodox faith, curls into leaves, spreads into branches, and overflows with the fruit of Christian fortitude. Crowned with the victorious Laurel against the thunderbolts of Maximinus—burying the glory of Tiberius Caesar, who wore the Laurel in a troubled sky—she takes heroic fortitude from the lightning of threats, courage from the scourges, goads from the wheel, and strength from the swords. She repels the assaulting North winds of the lead-weighted <note>a reference to lead-tipped whips</note> with the shield of her branches, and with her shading and dripping branches, she infuses the sap of the true faith into dead stumps, animating them into life, clothing them in greenness and the ornament of glory. But when the fire of fury in the breast of Maximinus, kindled by Stygian flames, burns again, the wild Tyranny burdens the Laurel with chains. Do you not know that the tall tree of Xerxes was honored, not burdened, by being bound with chains? The burning rage of the Tyrant subjects coals to the Laurel. Do you not know that the Laurel shines more illustriously from the rays of flames? Do you not know that the Laurel of the grove of Ammon, subjected to the hottest fires of the Pole, overflows in the greenness of its foliage? Do you not know that the Byzantine olive, sprinkled with a fiery rain, germinating with new leaves, spreads its top higher? Strip the Laurel, remove the bark, cut off the head. The milky neck will emanate snowy rivulets of milk, and from the spiked fountains of the veins, it will drip purple, so that it may quench the burning thirst of the Tyrant with Blood. And may the lily of virginal whiteness, related to the purple roses of the Martyrs, clearly manifest the Victorious Laurel CATHARINE, kin to the crowned Laurel. The Tyrant orders the crowned Laurel to be struck down by the executioner's steel. The crowned Laurel falls, prostrate in body, upright in countenance, sublime in spirit, higher than the earth, it rushes to the ground, so that it may crush with its body, trample with its feet, and elude with its breast whatever smells of the vanity of the fleeting earth. And because it is characteristic of the Laurel, when cut, it serves the triumph of those militant on earth and triumphant in heaven.</translation>

O most happy fecundity of the crowned Laurel CATHARINE, who, blessed with so many fruits, transmitted the fertile shoots of her followers to posterity. You would call this Laurel the tree of life, whose immortal vigor, in its mortal flower, showing the green hope of still-fruitful flowers, has gone forth from the ages and progresses into the ages, destined to lose neither its beauty through the old age of time, nor its greenness through the whirlwind of hostile storms, trading for immortal life through the very death of its flowers. She granted the bite of her fruit to the glutton of blood, Maximinus, that she might satisfy his voracious greed. They enter the arena. The empress, mistress of deceit and consort of the royal bed, emerges. Porphyrius, the supreme commander of wars, emerges, surrounded by two cohorts of soldiers. Maximinus, the Augustus and Emperor of the East, emerges, offering the tender Virgin honeyed enticements, blandishments, and allurements of pleasure, all more powerful for persuasion than any torture. How does CATHARINE respond to these things? With a brief but sharp address, she stripped the Empress, the wife of Maximinus, and Porphyrius, the invincible commander of the royal army, of the weapons of impiety, clothed them in the breastplate of justice and the helmet of salvation, and captured them in obedience to the faith. Virgil, the phoenix of geniuses, tells of the olive tree of Hercules which, dried up by the iniquity of time, prolific in no leaves and endowed with no greenery, joined to the Laurel, sprouted again with severed trunks, spread into branches, curled into leaves, and offered an opaque shade to travelers. So much did it benefit to be joined to the Laurel. Let us extract the kernel of truth from the husk of fables. The Empress, wife of Maximinus, who had withered in the sterile arena of paganism, joined to the crowned Laurel CATHARINE, took on the greenery of the orthodox faith, curled into leaves, spread into branches, and thrived in the fruit of Christian fortitude. Crowned with the victorious Laurel against the thunderbolts of Maximinus—the glory of Tiberius Caesar who wore a laurel in a troubled sky being buried—she takes heroic fortitude from the lightning of threats, courage from the scourges, goads from the wheel, and strength from the swords. She blunts the encroaching North winds of the lead-weighted <note>referring to whips tipped with lead</note> with the boss of her branches, and with her shading and dripping boughs, she infuses the juice of the true faith into dead stumps, animating them into life, clothing them in greenery and the ornament of glory. But as the fire of fury rekindled in the heart of Maximinus from Stygian fires, the savage tyrant burdens the Laurel with chains. Do you not know that the tall tree of Xerxes is honored, not burdened, by being bound with chains? The raging madness of the tyrant places coals beneath the Laurel. Do you not know that the Laurel shines more brightly from the rays of flames? Do you not know that the Laurel of the Ammonian grove, subjected to the most burning fires of the Pole, thrives in the greenery of its foliage? Do you not know that the Byzantine olive, sprinkled with a rain of flames, germinates with new leaves and extends its top higher? Strip the Laurel, remove the bark, truncate the neck. The milky neck will emanate white streams of milk, and from the spiked fountains of the veins, it will drip purple, so that it might quench the burning thirst of the tyrant with Blood. And the lilies of virginal whiteness, related to the purple roses of the Martyrs, the victorious Laurel CATHARINE, crowned and kin, shall lucently manifest. The tyrant orders the crowned Laurel to be struck down by the lictor’s steel. And what is peculiar to the Laurel is that, when cut, it serves the triumph of those militant on earth and triumphant in heaven.</translation>

Do you not know that the tall tree of Xerxes is honored, not burdened, by being bound with chains? The raging madness of the tyrant places coals beneath the Laurel. Do you not know that the Laurel shines more brightly from the rays of flames? Do you not know that the Laurel of the Ammonian grove, subjected to the most burning fires of the Pole, thrives in the greenery of its foliage? Do you not know that the Byzantine olive, sprinkled with a rain of flames, germinates with new leaves and extends its top higher? Strip the Laurel, remove the bark, truncate the neck. The milky neck will emanate white streams of milk, and from the spiked fountains of the veins, it will drip purple, so that it might quench the burning thirst of the tyrant with Blood. the union of the body, with the concord of its members under one spirit, constitutes the form of society; the intention of living well holds the proximate final cause; but the desire to attain the future holds the final intention, for the sake of which other things are established. From all this is gathered the necessity of an administration which conforms to that intention, carries it to its effect, and preserves it; and it is taught that a principate, just like a single spirit and the art of governing, is required no less than in a single physical body. Reason in the soul, and the intellect of things to be done, and of those things which ought to be entrusted to be executed by individual members. The members of one man are not suited for all actions, but must be preserved and informed under their own proper <note>functions</note>. The foot cannot see, the eye cannot walk, the ear cannot touch, the hand cannot hear, because it does not have the instrument or organ for that purpose. Nor does the soul, which knows the faculty and action of each member, order the same thing, but rather it commands its own proper <note>functions</note>, and thus it cares for individual things with proper solicitude. The prudent administration that presides over the body of society follows this example, and it provides for and procures what is appropriate for individual members or men. First and principally it considers the whole body of the people, then also the individuals, lest while it considers only the whole, having neglected the parts from which the whole is perfected, the whole itself should fail.
